To further test the necessity of the presence of a bona fide phosphate binding site for the catalytic activity of DERA, as well as the possibility of adapting DERA into also accepting non-phosphorylated acceptor aldehydes, we performed limited saturation mutagenesis using the NDT codon set to replace Ser238 and Ser239. The resulting variants were assayed for their ability to incorporate 14C-labeled acetaldehyde into the acceptor phenyl acetaldehyde (Fig. 3). The assay is not quantitative but useful for screening purposes, and the reaction illustrated in Fig. 3 was specifically chosen based on both commercial availability of the arylsubstituted aldehyde, and the current industrial interest in producing biocatalysts that can catalyse aldol addition.27,28 Fig. S2† shows a typical result from a screen of aldol addition activities in bacterial lysates from DERA-variant expressing cells. Sequence analysis of the scored hits revealed that Ser was no longer over-represented in the hits with apparent aldol addition activity. Rather, Ile displayed the highest over-representation at position 238, followed by Ser in second and Val in third places (Fig. S3†). The order of preferred residues at position 239 was Leu > Ile > His. Ser was absent at position 239 in all picked hit variants. Since these activity screens had targeted the aldol addition of acetaldehyde and phenyl acetaldehyde it was not obvious whether these DERA variants would retain activity with phosphorylated substrates such as dR5P. To test this, an Ile238/Ile239 variant was purified and analyzed for activity with dR5P. This mutant did indeed exhibit reasonable activity also with this phosphorylated substrate (Table 1), which clearly demonstrates that the Ser238/Ser239 pair is not critical for catalytic activity in and of itself.

Finally, in order to further explore the effect of mutations at positions 238 and 239 on overall structural stability, we performed molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of both wild-type DERA, and the S238P, S239P, S238P/S239P and S238I/S239I mutants in their substrate free forms. The simulation setup was as described in the Experimental section, and each variant was equilibrated for a total of 300 ns over 3 replicas with different initial velocities (100 ns each), leading to a total of 1.5 μs of cumulative simulation time for all variants. Fig. S4† shows the root mean square deviations of the backbone atoms for each variant, averaged over 3 replicas, demonstrating the convergence of the simulations. Following from this, we calculated root mean square fluctuations (RMSF) along the MD trajectories for each individual variant (Fig. 5), as well as calculating dynamic cross correlation maps (DCCM) from the MD trajectories, using the Bio3D package.29,30

From the RMSF plot, it can be seen that the enzyme is fairly flexible, with each peak on the RMSF plots corresponding to a different helix in DERA (see Fig. 5 for a colour coded comparison of the different helices of DERA and each peak on the RMSF plot), thus corresponding to “breathing motions” of this enzyme. As can be seen from these plots, the introduction of all mutants dampens the flexibility of the enzyme in several regions, and, in particular, the S239P mutant shows less flexibility around residues 25–75, 170–180 and 220–230 (see Fig. 5 for colouring). Following from this, a side-by-side comparison of the DCCM plots for the wild-type and S239P type mutant forms of DERA (Fig. 6) show that this substitution leads to a substantial loss in, in particular, anti-correlated motions. Interestingly, if one then extends this to placing all variants shown in Table 1 side by side, and ranking them according to their measured kcat/KM values, it can be seen that this loss of anti-correlated motions follows a clear trend across the mutants, with the variants with the lowest kcat/KM values (i.e. S238P and the S238P/S239P and S238I/S239I double mutants) showing much lower correlated motions (Fig. S5†). This is in good agreement with previous work that suggested the presence of coupled networks of residues in enzymes that play a role in enzyme function (e.g.ref. 10–17 among many others), and in particular work by Bruice which argues for anti-correlated motions as a driving force in catalysis.31 Therefore, the introduction of the mutations at positions 238 and 239 appears to alter the enzyme's dynamics, rigidifying it, which will in turn lead it to sample fewer catalytically active conformations and impair both substrate binding and subsequent TS stabilization, as shown also in the trends in kcat/KM in Table 1.

DERA's requirement for phosphorylated substrates can be due to different reasons. (1) The obvious, and most trivial reason is to function as a negatively charged anchor binding to a complementary binding site, thereby increasing the affinity for the substrate in the ground state and throughout the reaction. This could be argued as being particularly important for small substrate molecules such as G3P. Any contribution to substrate selectivity, however, is questionable since the relatively strong binding interactions between the protein and phosphate moiety may overshadow the weaker (e.g. hydrogen bonding) interactions that steers substrate selectivity, including stereoselectivity. (2) Extensive experimental work by Richard and co-workers on other enzymes acting on phosphorylated substrates, which include orotidine monophosphate decarboxylase32–34 and triosephosphate isomerase,35–37 shows that remote protein–phosphodianion interactions can, in these cases, be crucial for transition state stabilization, in part by promoting the formation of (and stabilizing of) active high-energy conformations of the protein. (3) In the current case of DERA catalysed aldol cleavage of dR5P, the additional ring opening of the predominantly existing furanose form (99.8%38) of the aldose substrate to the reactive open-chain aldehyde has to be considered (the concentration of the aldehyde in solution is expected to be even lower than 0.2% of the total dR5P, since it will be further equilibrated with the hydrated gem-diol). The phosphate group on the furanose may in this case act as an affinity tag facilitating imperfect binding to the active site in which subsequent ring opening is catalysed. The ring opening can be facilitated both by acid catalysis but also by allowing for new binding interactions once the sugar is in the open-chain form, and the aldehyde thus formed is trapped as the imine intermediate after attack by Lys167.

For comparison, note that phosphoglucose isomerase, which catalyses the isomerization of glucose-1-phosphate and fructose-1-phosphate faces the same problem. This enzyme acts on the open chain of the aldose or ketose substrates, while these sugars are present in the respective pyranose and furanose forms in aqueous solution, to an even higher degree than in dR5P. Crystal structures have been solved in which both the cyclized and the open-chain form of the substrates can be observed within the same active site. In this enzyme, a His residue has been suggested to be the acid catalyst for sugar ring opening once bound within the active site.39 There is no residue in DERA that corresponds to the catalytic His residue present in phosphoglucose isomerase, but rather, there is a strategically positioned water molecule aligned in a hydrogen-bonding network involving the O4 of the open-chain Schiff base and the ammonium of Lys172 (PDB ID: 1JCJ7,8), suggesting possible acid functionality. The uncatalyzed ring-opening of furanoses is comparably slow, with rates well below 1 s−1.40,41 This is at least 15-fold below the value of kcat for cleavage of dR5P by DERA (Table 1). Hence, catalysed ring-opening must exceed at least the value of the turnover number. Phosphorylation, however, considerably increases the ring-opening rate (40–100 s−1for R5P, depending on anomer).42 The ring-opening of dR5P is therefore not expected to be rate-limiting to any extent. The aldehyde thus formed is trapped as the imine intermediate after attack by Lys167.

Conclusions
In conclusion, in the present work, we have performed a combined experimental and computational study of the effect of mutagenesis of Ser238 and Ser239 on the structural dynamics and resulting phosphodianion stabilization of DERA. We demonstrate that although site-saturation mutagenesis suggests that the specific presence of a Ser at these positions is less important for the catalytic activity of the enzyme (as other residues still showed some activity), nevertheless, by substituting Ser for Pro at these positions, we dampen the dynamics of the enzyme with a concomitant loss in both TS entropy and catalytic activity. Additionally, the structural fluctuations of the wild-type enzyme appear to be highly (anti-) correlated, and the loss of catalytic activity appears to be directly connected to the loss of these correlated motions. Therefore, we demonstrate here a critical role for the interplay between coupled motions, entropic changes and flexibility in driving the catalytic activity of this enzyme, and postulate that these features can be regulated for targeted engineering of DERA to accept new substrates.

Experimental
A detailed description of the experimental is given in the ESI,† and also described briefly below.

Enzyme production, mutagenesis and kinetic characterization
The coding region of the DERA gene was obtained by colony PCR from E. coli XL1-Blue, and the amplified fragment was inserted into the pGT7 expression vector.43 Mutations were introduced by overlap mutagenesis PCR with the wild-type DERA gene as template. See Table S1† for oligonucleotide sequences. DERA genes, wild-type and mutants, were transformed into E. coli BL21-AI (Invitrogen) for protein expression. Screening of the NDT-mutated gene library for expression of DERA variants with aldol addition activity with acetaldehyde and phenyl acetaldehyde was performed in 96-well plate format, essentially as described in ref. 44, but with modifications for the current expression vector and host cell. Aldolase activity upon incorporating 14C-labeled acetaldehyde was detected after separation by thin layer chromatography followed by autoradiography, of the reaction mixtures after incubation of DERA-variant expressing bacterial lysate with labelled and cold acetaldehyde and phenyl acetaldehyde (Fig. S2†).

Purification of DERA variants was accomplished through nickel IMAC, as previously described.43 The purified protein was stored in 50 mM triethanolamine buffer, pH 8.0. The rates of catalysed aldol cleavage of dR5P were assayed as described in ref. 45, and steady state kinetic parameters were determined after fitting the Michaelis–Menten equation to the data using SIMFIT (http://www.simfit.org.uk). In addition, catalyzed rates, under saturating (kcat) or unsaturating (kcat/KM) conditions, in the presence of wild-type DERA or the S239P mutant, were determined at different temperatures (15 °C, 20 °C, 25 °C, 30 °C, 38 °C and 45 °C). The natural logarithms of the ratios of the determined rates were plotted as functions of the inverse of T to allow for extraction of the changes in transition state enthalpy and entropy (eqn (1)), caused by the S239P mutation.

The steady state kinetic parameters for wild-type DERA, and the S239P and S238I/S239I mutants were also determined at pH values of 7, 8 and 9. The results are presented in Fig. S1 and Table S2.†

Computational approaches
All molecular dynamics simulations of DERA were performed using the Q simulation package46 and the OPLS-AA force field.47 The 0.99 Å resolution structure of wild-type DERA (PDB ID: 1P1X8,9) was used as the starting point for all simulations, and the relevant mutations were introduced to this structure using Richardson's common-atom rotamer library48 as implemented in the UCSF Chimera software package. In each case, the system was solvated using a 35 Å sphere of TIP3P water molecules, with a 10 kcal mol−1 Å−2 positional restraint on the 15% outer layer of the solvent sphere to stabilize it during the simulation, which is necessary using spherical boundary conditions (see also e.g. our recent work49,50). All residues (apart from the Schiff base) were protonated according to their preferred protonation state at physiological pH, resulting in an overall system charge of −5, which was neutralized with Na+ counterions. After initial solvation, the system was gradually heated from 0 to 300 K over the course of 1 ns using a 1 fs timestep and the Berendsen thermostat.51 The structure was subject to an initial positional restraint of 200 kcal mol−1 Å−2 on all heavy atoms to allow protons to equilibrate to their optimal positions and remove initial bad contacts in the crystal structure, and this restraint was gradually dropped during the heating procedure, as the structure was allowed to relax. After this initial equilibration, we ran a further 100 ns production run, using 3 replicas for each system with different initial velocities (i.e. 300 ns simulation time per system) The only restraint kept in the actual production run was a weak 3 kcal mol−1 Å−2 positional restraint on the Na+ counterions to keep them within the simulation sphere. This procedure was performed on both the wild-type enzyme as well as the S238P, S239P, S238P/S239P and S238I/S239I mutants, and the final 100 ns of each trajectory were retained for further analysis. All analysis was performed externally by importing our Q trajectories into GROMACS,52 with the exception of the dynamic cross correlation analysis, which was performed using the Bio3D package.29,30

Determinants of substrate specificity in D-3-phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase. Conversion of the M. tuberculosis enzyme from one that does not use α-ketoglutarate as a substrate to one that does

Abstract
d-3-Phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PGDH) converts d-3-phosphoglycerate (PGA) to phosphohydroxypyruvate (PHP) in the first step of l-serine biosynthesis. This reaction is reversible, and some PGDHs are capable of using α-ketoglutarate (αKG) instead of PHP in the reverse direction to produce α-hydroxyglutarate. The enzymes so far shown to have this ability are Type II PGDHs, suggesting that this may be a common feature of the Type II enzymes. Type I PGDHs examined so far do not share this feature. Inspection of PGDH sequences shows that a GCFCI … WXKX motif is commonly found in Type II PGDHs while a GRAGT … WXRX motif is commonly associated with Type I PGDHs. The removal of the cationic side chain at the first position shown above in the Type I PGDH from Mycobacterium tuberculosis converts it to an enzyme capable of using αKG where the native enzyme is not. It also produces an enzyme that regenerates NAD+ in the forward reaction when coupled to phosphoserine aminotransferase, as was previously shown for E. coli PGDH. Substitution of an arginyl residue for a lysyl residue at the second position of ecPGDH, decreases the kcat/Km of the enzyme by approximately 50-fold when using αKG, but only approximately 3-fold when using PHP. This suggests that a PGDH dependent cycle that conserves NAD+ in E. coli may be operative in many other organisms expressing the GCFCI … WXKX motif.

1. Introduction
d -3-Phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PGDH) catalyzes the first step in the synthesis of l-serine by converting the glycolytic intermediate, d-3-phosphoglycerate (PGA), to phosphohydroxypyruvate (PHP). Subsequently, PHP is converted to phosphoserine (PS) by phosphoserine aminotransferase (PSAT) and then PS is converted to l-serine by phosphoserine phosphatase (PSP) (Scheme 1). Since the equilibrium of the reaction catalyzed by PGDH lies well in the direction of PGA production [1], the enzyme is often assayed in the so called “reverse” direction using PHP and NADH as substrates.
Three types of PGDH, distinguishable by their domain content and quaternary structure, have been identified [2,3]. All three types contain a substrate binding domain and a nucleotide binding domain. These are the only domains that occur in Type III PGDHs. Type II PGDHs contain an additional ACT domain, and Type I PGDHs contain an ACT domain and an ASB domain. Type I and Type II PGDHs are tetramers formed by subunit interaction between ACT domains, while Type III PGDHs are dimers because they lack ACT domains. l-serine binds at the ACT domain interfaces and inhibits catalytic activity in those PGDHs that are sensitive to l-serine, such as PGDH from Escherichia coli (ecPGDH) and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (mtPGDH). The ASB domain of some PGDHs, such as mtPGDH, contains a region rich in cationic amino acid side chains that binds certain anions that play a role in modulating the enzymes sensitivity to l-serine [4,5]. However, not all PGDHs that contain ACT and/or ASB domains display the requisite functions because they may not contain the necessary amino acid residues required to carry out those functions.
In 1996, Zhao and Winkler showed that PGDH from E. coli could also utilize α-ketoglutarate (αKG) in the reverse direction as a substrate in place of PHP [6], resulting in the production of d-2-hydroxyglutarate (d2HG). It was recently demonstrated that PGDH from Pseudomonas stutzeri (psPGDH, 7) and Saccharomyces cerevisiae (scPGDH, 8, 9) could also utilize αKG as a substrate in the same manner as ecPGDH. ecPGDH and psPGDH have also been shown to purify with tightly bound NADH [7,10,11], leading to the proposal [12] that the reaction with αKG is necessary for serine synthesis to proceed in vivo since the forward reaction requires NAD+. In this regard, the ability of ecPGDH to utilize αKG as a substrate in the reverse direction has recently been shown to be part of a self-sustaining cycle that results in the preservation of NAD+ [13].
ecPGDH, psPGDH, and scPGDH are all Type II enzymes, suggesting that the ability to utilize αKG may be a trait of Type II PGDHs in general, although a larger sampling will be necessary to confirm this. The Type I and Type III PGDHs have been reported to not be able to utilize αKG as a substrate [13]. A possible exception to this is the human enzyme (hsPGDH) where a very low level of activity has been reported [14]. However, this activity is present at a very low level and it has been shown [13] that it is not sufficient to maintain the NAD+ preserving cycle that is active in ecPGDH [15].
An inspection of the amino acid sequences of the three types of PGDH in the region of the active site shows an amino acid substitution of an arginine residue in Type I and Type III enzymes in place of a cysteine residue in Type II enzymes (Fig. 1, position 129). Fig. 2 shows the structures of the active sites with bound substrate for mtPGDH and ecPGDH that have been determined by crystallography and show that the ligand is bound in basically the same orientation. The structures clearly indicate the residues that interact with functional groups at opposite ends of the substrate. Arg 72 in mtPGDH protrudes into the active site pocket with the guanidinium group in hydrogen bonding distance of the carboxyl and/or alpha keto group of the substrate. On the other hand, the cysteine residue in ecPGDH does not interact with the substrate as its sulfhydryl group is oriented away from the substrate. In addition, in Type I and Type II PGDHs, a cationic residue from the adjacent subunit protrudes into the active sight where it interacts with the substrate (Fig. 1, position 189). This is usually a lysyl residue in Type II PGDHs (Lys 141 in ecPGDH) and an arginyl residue in Type I PGDHs (Arg 132 in mtPGDH). Other residues at the respective active sites that are in position to interact with substrate are generally conserved. In contrast, although the Type III PGDHs may possess a cationic residue at, or near, this sequence location in the adjacent subunit, the available crystal structures show that this cationic residue does not interact with substrate in the adjacent active site.
The correlation of the lack of a basic residue (Fig. 1, position 129) at the corresponding position in those enzymes that can utilize αKG as a substrate suggests that this residue may play an important role in determining substrate specificity in PGDH enzymes. In this investigation, the pertinent residues at the active sites of ecPGDH and mtPGDH were probed with site-specific mutagenesis and demonstrated that removal of a cationic side chain at the position of Arg 72 (position 129 in Fig. 1) in mtPGDH successfully converted it from an enzyme not capable of using αKG as a substrate into one that can. It also demonstrated that the modified mtPGDH acts similarly to ecPGDH in that the forward reaction can no longer be monitored by absorbance at 340 nm showing that there is no net production of NADH. ecPGDH is capable of maintaining a cycle that preserves NAD+ by utilizing αKG from the next step in the pathway. This result suggests the same is true for the modified mtPGDHs. An examination of the sequences of PGDH enzymes from various species shows that Type II PGDHs almost always lack the arginyl residue at position 129 while it is most often present in Type I PGDHs. This observation may provide one factor in predicting which PGDH enzymes may be able to utilize αKG, and possibly also which utilize a cycle for conserving NAD+.
2. Experimental procedures
The cloning, expression, and purification of PGDH from E. coli and M. tuberculosis have been described previously [16]. Both were expressed with hexa-histidine tags at the amino terminus and purified using metal affinity chromatography. All assays were performed in 100 mM potassium phosphate buffer, pH 7.0, and activity in the “reverse” direction was determined by monitoring the change in absorbance of NADH at 340 nm using either αKG or PHP as substrate. The kinetic parameters were determined by fitting the data from velocity versus substrate concentration plots to the Michaelis-Menton equation modified for direct determination of kcat,
where kcat is the maximum velocity (Vmax) divided by the enzyme concentration [E]t, S is the substrate concentration and Km is the substrate concentration at half maximum velocity. The fit shown in Fig. 3C is performed with the Michaelis-Menton equation plus a linear term. When substrate inhibition occurred, the plots were fit using the standard equation for substrate inhibition [16],
where Ki is the inhibition constant. Enzyme concentration was determined by absorbance at 280 nm using the extinction coefficients of 29,515 L/mol-cm and 25,565 L/mol-cm for ecPGDH and mtPGDH, respectively. “Forward” direction assays were conducted by coupling PGDH with PSAT in the presence of saturating substrates. The assays shown in Fig. 4 contained saturating concentrations of PGA (9 mM), NAD+ (5 mM), and glutamate (20 mM).
PCR based site-specific mutagenesis was performed as previously described [17] and verified by DNA sequence analysis of the whole gene. Protein sequence alignments were performed with the EXPASY ClustlO (Uniprot) program found at www.uniprot.org/align/and edited manually where gaps occurred to maximize homology.

3. Results
Representative amino acid sequences of the three PGDH types from various species are presented in Fig. 1. Included in this figure are the sequences of the three enzymes that have been shown to possess activity with αKG as substrate, those from Escherichia coli [13], Pseudomonas stutzeri [7], and Saccharomyces cerevisiae [8]. Of the other types, PGDH from Mycobacterium tuberculosis [18], Rattus norvegicus [19], and Entamoeba hystolytica [20,21] have been shown to lack this activity. Although that from Homo sapiens has been reported to utilize αKG, the activity is very low, with a kcat of ~0.08 sec−1 which is ~400 times lower than that for ecPGDH [14]. As mentioned earlier, hsPGDH is not capable of generating sufficient NAD+ from αKG to maintain the NAD+ conserving cycle that is active in ecPGDH.
In order to investigate the role of Arg 72 (position 129) in mtPGDH, site specific mutagenesis was employed to substitute the arginyl side chain in mtPGDH with other selected amino acid side chains. The results, shown in Table 1, demonstrate that removal of the cationic group of Arg 72 (position 129) in mtPGDH converts the enzyme from one that cannot utilize αKG to one that can. Replacement of the arginyl side chain with a lysyl side chain failed to accomplish this, showing that a cationic side chain at this position renders the enzyme unable to use αKG. The cysteine residues in ecPGDH do not interact with the substrate (see Fig. 2). Cys81 (position 129 in Fig. 2), the residue that corresponds to R72 in mtPGDH, is too far removed from the active site and the sulfhydryl of the other cysteine (Cys83) is pointed away from the substrate and is also too far removed. Furthermore, earlier work [22] where these cysteines were converted to alanine residues showed that they do not contribute to substrate binding. Since the R72A mutation in mtPGDH showed activity with αKG, it was concluded that it is the absence of a positive charge that allows interaction with αKG and not the presence of cysteine. It is not surprising that the Km s for mtR72A and mtR72L are relatively high since the active site of mtPGDH is exquisitely tuned to use PHP as the substrate showing a 200 fold increase in kcat relative to ecPGDH in the native enzymes. Interestingly, as shown in Table 2 and Fig. 3, the mtPGDH R72A, R72L, and R72K mutations also resulted in an enzyme that appeared to be nearly unsaturable with respect to PHP concentrations (Fig. 3) that displayed substrate inhibition in the native enzyme. Higher PHP concentrations were not employed due to the cost and limited availability of the reagent.

Replacement of this cationic group in mtPGDH also mimicked the activity of ecPGDH when assayed in the forward direction. Fig. 4 demonstrates that like ecPGDH, there is little net change in NADH levels, as monitored by absorbance of NADH at 340 nm, when mtPGDH R72A is used. It is only when active native mtPGDH is added to the reaction mixture that significant net NADH production can be observed. ecPGDH preserved NAD+ by utilizing the αKG that is formed by the conversion of glutamate to αKG by PSAT, the second enzyme in the l-serine biosynthetic pathway (2, Scheme 1). It was previously shown [13] that net production of NADH is observed when native mtPGDH is included in the assay because the rate of conversion of PHP to PS by native mtPGDH is faster than the rate of conversion of αKG to PGA by ecPGDH. These results for mtR72A PGDH indicate the same is likely true for mtPGDH when the cationic side chain is removed at this position. However, it is not possible to verify this directly since an assay is not available to measure the rate of mtPGDH R72A alone in the forward direction. Nonetheless, it seems likely since the rate of αKG conversion in the reverse direction, when substrates are saturating, is 8-fold higher for mtPGDH R72A than for native ecPGDH.
Another apparently consistent difference between Type I and Type II PGDHs is that Type I PGDHs have an arginyl residue and Type II PGDHs have a lysyl residues protruding into the active site from the adjacent subunit (position 291 in Fig. 1). Conversion of Arg 132 to a lysyl residue in mtPGDH does not alter its lack of activity toward αKG, but does decrease the Km for PHP by approximately 10-fold.
Conversion of Lys 141 to an arginyl side chain (K141R) in ecPGDH has no effect on the Km and only a small effect on the kcat of the enzyme for PHP (~3-fold increase), but increases the Km of ecPGDH for αKG by approximately 10-fold while decreasing the kcat by approximately 4-fold. This results in an approximate 48-fold decrease of the kcat/Km for αKG but only an approximate 3-fold increase in kcat/Km for PHP.
The double mutant, mtR72A R132K, resulted in an enzyme with no measurable activity with αKG and one that displayed good activity and substrate inhibition with PHP. Interestingly, with both substrates, it is the characteristics of the R132K mutation that predominate. The activity with PHP displays a comparable kcat and Ki, but increases the Km by approximately 10-fold.
All attempts to introduce an arginyl residue into ecPGDH at or near the location of the cysteine residues resulted in no detectable expression of enzyme.

4. Discussion
The data show that removing the cationic side chain of Arg72 in mtPGDH produces an enzyme that now utilizes αKG as a substrate when the native enzyme did not. Since the reaction in the forward direction is no longer able to be monitored by observing the generation of NADH, the modified mtPGDHs act similarly to ecPGDH which uses endogenous αKG generated by PSAT in the coupled reaction to convert NADH back to NAD+ [13].
The kcat/Km of the resulting mtPGDH enzyme is approximately an order of magnitude less than that for ecPGDH, suggesting the greatest effect is with substrate binding interactions prior to catalysis. In fact, the kcat for mtPGDH R72A is ~8 fold higher than that for ecPGDH. Lys141 in ecPGDH also plays a significant role in utilizing αKG as a substrate since the presence of an arginyl residue at this position in ecPGDH decreases the kcat/Km by approximately 50-fold.
While the conversion of Arg72 to another residue in mtPGDH allows αKG to be used as a substrate, it also decreases the enzyme's ability to use PHP as a substrate. With native mtPGDH, the velocity of the reaction with PHP reaches a maximum at approximately 0.2 mM substrate before evidence for substrate inhibition is apparent. However, the velocity of the reaction at 0.2 mM PHP for the relevant mutants is considerably lower and increases in a seemingly unsaturable manner at least up to very high relative concentrations of PHP. This suggests that the Km for the reaction with PHP is greatly negatively affected while the catalysis proceeds at a significant pace once substrate is bound in the active site in the proper configuration. The concentration of the enzyme tetramer in the reactions with mtPGDH R72A, mtPGDH R72L, and native mtPGDH is 0.55 μM, 0.3 μM, and 0.0025 μM, respectively. This suggests that the kcat is reduced as much as 100-200 fold for the mutated enzymes. A reduction of the kcat for mtPGDH by ~200 fold would result in a value approximating that for native ecPGDH. Therefore, while the mutations in mtPGDH produce enzymes with an active site better suited to accept αKG, their ability to interact productively with PHP is diminished to a level more similar to native ecPGDH.
The three enzymes that have so far been shown to utilize αKG as a substrate are Type II PGDHs from E. coli, P. stutzeri and S. cerevisiae. The first two are prokaryotes, specifically γ-proteobacteria, while the latter is a unicellular eukaryote. The three different “Types” of PGDH are distinguished on the basis of their secondary structure, namely the presence or absence of the ACT and ASB structural domains, and are found in widely varying species. For instance, Type I enzymes are found in bacteria as well as vertebrates and Type II enzymes are found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms. It was therefore of interest to examine whether or not the sequence differences at the catalytic sites examined in this investigation were also conserved with respect to structural type. Table 3 presents examples of all three PGDH types from bacteria to vertebrates along with the sequence motifs where differences are found relative to the C/R substitution at position 129 in Fig. 1 in the GCFCI/GRAGA motif and the K/R substitution at position 189 in Fig. 1 at the WXKX/WXRX motif. Although not exhaustive, and while a few exceptions were found, the entries presented show that the GCFI … WXKX motif is predominately associated with Type II enzymes which predominate in the γ-proteobacteria. On the other hand, the GRAGA … WXRX motif is usually associated with Type I enzymes which are predominant in the higher order organisms. The Type III enzymes, on the other hand, do not show any consistent pattern and often lack one or both motifs. Although there are a few exceptions in the correlation of sequence motif with enzyme type, based on the structural features noted for each enzyme type in the introduction, the presence or absence of an arginyl residue at position 129 (R72 in mtPGDH), is likely a good predictor of whether or not the enzyme can utilize αKG as a substrate.

The demonstration in E. coli that the ability to use αKG is associated with a cycle that conserves the coenzyme NAD+, suggests that the same cycle may be operative in those organisms whose PGDH has the conserved motif. While it was not directly demonstrated, Zhang et al. suggested that this may be the case for PGDH from Pseudomonas stutzeri [7]. It will be interesting to see if the conservation of the “E. coli motif” is always associated with such a cycle regardless of the structural type in which it is found. If, like E. coli, a significant portion of their carbon passes through the l-serine biosynthetic pathway, it would presumably impart a significant “redox” advantage to those organisms by maintaining a favorable NAD+/NADH ratio [9] that is not jeopardized by the significant flux of the l-serine biosynthetic pathway.

Structures and activities of widely conserved small prokaryotic aminopeptidases-P clarify classification of M24B peptidases

Abstract
M24B peptidases cleaving Xaa-Pro bond in dipeptides are prolidases whereas those cleaving this bond in longer peptides are aminopeptidases-P. Bacteria have small aminopeptidases-P (36-39 kDa), which are diverged from canonical aminopeptidase-P of Escherichia coli (50 kDa). Structure-function studies of small aminopeptidases-P are lacking. We report crystal structures of small aminopeptidases-P from E. coli and Deinococcus radiodurans, and report substrate-specificities of these proteins and their ortholog from Mycobacterium tuberculosis. These are aminopeptidases-P, structurally close to small prolidases except for absence of dipeptide-selectivity loop. We noticed absence of this loop and conserved arginine in canonical archaeal prolidase (Maher et al., Biochemistry. 43, 2004, 2771-2783) and questioned its classification. Our enzymatic assays show that this enzyme is an aminopeptidase-P. Further, our mutagenesis studies illuminate importance of DXRY sequence motif in bacterial small aminopeptidases-P and suggest common evolutionary origin with human XPNPEP1/XPNPEP2. Our analyses reveal sequence/structural features distinguishing small aminopeptidases-P from other M24B peptidases.

1 INTRODUCTION
Most peptidases cannot hydrolyze the Xaa-Pro iminopeptide bond (Xaa = any amino acid) because of restricted rotation around phi dihedral angle. Specialized peptidases from MEROPS1 M24B family are known to hydrolyze the Xaa-Pro iminopeptide bond at the N-terminus of peptide substrates. These enzymes are the metallopeptidases with conserved dinuclear active site. M24B peptidases that exclusively hydrolyze Xaa-Pro peptide bond in dipeptides are called prolidases (EC: 3.4.13.9), whereas those that preferentially hydrolyze this bond in longer peptides are called aminopeptidases-P (EC: 3.4.11.9).2, 3 Aminopeptidases-P are widely conserved and have been reported from bacteria and eukaryotes.4, 5 Overall, the role of M24B peptidases in eukaryotes is well documented. For instance, human XPNPEP2 has been identified as a key inactivator of bradykinin peptide, a potent vasodilator, and cardioprotective hormone.4, 6, 7 Human XPNPEP3 is associated with cystic-kidney disease8 and TNF-TNFR2 cellular signaling,9 and its yeast and plant orthologs (Intermediate cleavage peptidase 55) have been shown to process many mitochondrial matrix proteins for their stabilization.10-12 Aminopeptidase-P from Plasmodium falciparum is an essential enzyme and is proposed to have a role in vacuolar catabolism of hemoglobin and cytosolic peptide turnover, and it has been identified as a potential drug target.13, 14 In bacteria, aminopeptidases-P have been shown to be important for the recycling of proline in Salmonella typhimurium.15 In Bacillus subtillis, the genes encoding aminopeptidase-P (pepA) and prolidase (pepB) have been shown to be involved in increasing the concentration of L-proline inside the cells leading to their osmoprotection.16 Aminopeptidases-P are also important for the food and beverage industry. For instance, aminopeptidase-P from Lactococcus lactis is an important enzyme in the cheese-making process for removing bitterness by hydrolyzing proline-containing peptides.17

The aminopeptidase-P from Escherichia coli (50 kDa; AMPP-Ec) was the first member of M24B family for which the crystal structure was reported.18 It is a well-studied enzyme and is considered as a canonical aminopeptidase-P. The further structural studies of aminopeptidases-P have categorized them into two classes. Aminopeptidases-P from E. coli (AMPP-Ec, PDB ID: 1A16)18 and human (XPNPEP3, PDB ID: 5XEV)11 have two domains, whereas other aminopeptidases-P from human (XPNPEP1; PDB ID: 3CTZ),19 Caenorhabditis elegans (PDB ID: 4S2R),20 and P. falciparum (PDB ID: 5JQK)13 have three domains. Both types of aminopeptidases-P have conserved catalytic C-terminal domains. However, the N-terminal domains are not as conserved in these proteins. Interestingly, a distinct class of aminopeptidases-P (small aminopeptidases-P) have been purified and enzymatically characterized from E. coli and three subspecies of Lactococcus lactis.5, 17, 21, 22 The size of the polypeptide in the small aminopeptidases-P (~36-39 kDa) is considerably smaller as compared to that of two-domain aminopeptidases-P (48-50 kDa) and three domain aminopeptidases-P (70-88 kDa). The structure-function studies of none of the small aminopeptidases-P have been reported yet. BLAST search shows that homologs of small aminopeptidases-P with similar polypeptide sizes are widely conserved in bacteria and archaea. Some of these homologs are identified as bacterial and archaeal prolidases based on the sequence motif (XER) proposed by Are et al.23 Zheng et al. identified DXRY sequence motif in the N-terminal region of small aminopeptidase-P from E. coli (Ec-smAPP) and its homologs.22 They showed that while the mutagenesis of the residues of DXRY motif did not change substrate specificity profiles of Ec-smAPP, it did knock-down its methionyl aminopeptidase activity against the substrate Met-Ala-Ser. Based on conservation of the motif, it is likely to be important for the enzyme, however, its role is not clearly understood. Sequence search of Ec-smAPP against Protein Data Bank (PDB) yielded two protein structures with the DXRY motif. Interestingly, one of these structures was annotated as a prolidase (PDB ID: 3Q6D) and the other was annotated as an aminopeptidase-P (PDB ID: 2ZSG). This shows that there is a subtle conflict in the annotation of these enzymes which has not been resolved because neither protein has been enzymatically characterized. In order to address this conflict in annotation and also to investigate the importance of the DXRY motif, we selected three proteins with DXRY motif that we believed were small aminopeptidases-P and carried out enzymatic and structural studies. These proteins are from evolutionarily diverged bacterial species (Ec-smAPP from E. coli, Dr-smAPP from Deinococcus radiodurans, and Mt-smAPP from Mycobacterium tuberculosis).

Here, we report the crystal structures of two of the chosen proteins (Ec-smAPP and Dr-smAPP) and enzymatic characterization of all three of them. We indeed found all the three enzymes to be aminopeptidases-P. Site-directed mutagenesis studies of Dr-smAPP showed that the DXRY motif is in fact important for enzymatic activity. Based on further analyses we suspected that the enzyme characterized as the canonical prolidase from archaea (Pf-peptidase from Pyrococcus furiosus)24, 25 could also hydrolyze larger peptides and hence be an aminopeptidase-P, not prolidase as reported earlier. We confirmed this by activity assays. Thus, we have identified structural and sequence features that can distinguish small aminopeptidases-P from other M24B peptidases.

2 MATERIALS AND METHODS
2.1 Cloning and protein purification
The DNA encoding small aminopeptidases-P from E. coli (Ec-smAPP; UniProt accession ID. P76524), D. radiodurans R1 (Dr-smAPP; UniProt accession ID. Q9RUY4) and M. tuberculosis (Mt-smAPP; UniProt accession ID. I6YDN6) as well as peptidase from P. furiosus (Pf-peptidase; UniProt accession ID. P81535) were amplified by PCR using thermostable Pfu DNA polymerase from the corresponding genomic DNA. The amplified genes were cloned into T7-promoter-based expression vector, pST50Tr, so as to form in-frame translational fusion proteins with StreptII-6xhistidine-tobacco etch virus protease site (STRHISTEV) tag.26 The coding region in each construct was verified by DNA sequencing. Six individual point mutations (D53A, R55A, Y56A, H193A, H281A, and R298A) in Dr-smAPP encoding plasmid were carried out using Quick-change site-directed mutagenesis method. For expression of individual proteins, the recombinant plasmids were transformed into E. coli BL21(DE3) pLysS expression host. The freshly transformed cells were grown overnight and were diluted by 100-fold for further growth in fresh media. The culture was grown at 37°C to OD600 ~0.3 then further incubated at 28°C. The cells were induced at OD600 ~0.8 for 18 hours with 0.2 mM isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG). All the proteins (Ec-smAPP, Dr-smAPP, and Pf-peptidase) expressed well and were found in the soluble fractions of the cell lysate except Mt-smAPP, which was found as inclusion bodies. To obtain soluble Mt-smAPP protein, heat shock treatment was given to the cells prior to induction of the culture. The cells growing at log phase at 37°C were shifted to 42°C for 30 minutes and then 18°C for 30 minutes. The culture was induced by IPTG at 28°C for 18 hours. For purification of all the proteins mentioned in the study, the corresponding cells were harvested by centrifugation at ambient temperature. The cell pellet was suspended in P300 buffer (50 mM sodium phosphate buffer, pH 7.0, 300 mM NaCl) and flash frozen in liquid nitrogen. Later, the cells were thawed and lysed by sonication. The desired proteins were purified using Ni-immobilized metal ion affinity chromatography (Ni-IMAC) technique. The bound protein was eluted with P300 buffer containing 500 mM imidazole at 4°C. The eluted proteins were dialyzed against T200 (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 200 mM NaCl). The fusion peptide tags were removed from the Ec-smAPP and Dr-smAPP proteins by TEV protease. These two proteins were further purified using His-Trap (5 mL) column on AKTA system (GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL) at ambient temperature. Protein samples were concentrated to ~15 mg ml−1 using ultrafiltration and supplemented with 20% (vol/vol) glycerol before storing at −70°C till further use.

2.2 Crystallization, data collection, and refinement
For the crystallization experiments, required amount of proteins (Ec-smAPP or Dr-smAPP) were purified through size-exclusion chromatography with T200 buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 200 mM NaCl) on Superdex 200, 10/300 GL column on AKTA purifier system (GE Healthcare). Both the proteins eluted as homodimers (Supporting Information Figure S1). The purified protein samples were concentrated to ~15 mg ml−1 for setting up crystallization trials. The crystallization was carried out at 21°C by making use of under oil microbatch method,27 in which 2 μL of protein solution was mixed with 2 μL of crystallization solution and overlaid with 50 μL of Al's oil (silicon fluid: mineral oil, 1:1, vol/vol) in 96-well U-bottom plates. Initial crystals of Ec-smAPP and Dr-smAPP were observed in 5 to 7 different crystallization conditions within 3 days. Crystal quality was improved by optimization of the initial conditions. The diffraction quality crystals of Dr-smAPP were grown in 0.1 M phospho-citrate pH 4.6, 0.2 M NaCl, and 22% PEG 8000 and those of Ec-smAPP were grown in 1.4 M trisodium citrate, 0.1 M sodium cacodylate, pH 6.5, 10% glycerol, and 0.5 mM ZnCl2. For obtaining metal-bound crystals of Dr-smAPP, crystallization solutions were supplemented with ZnCl2 to a final concentration of about 2 mM and incubated for 24 hours before harvesting. Crystals were cryoprotected by supplementing crystallization condition with 20% glycerol and flash frozen in liquid nitrogen. X-ray diffraction data were collected on beamline PX-BL21, Indus-2 (RRCAT, Indore, India).28

Diffraction images were integrated and scaled using XDS.29 Structures were solved by molecular replacement (MR) using PHASER30 suite on the CCP431 platform. The MR model was prepared by Chainsaw32 using the putative prolidase from T. sibiricus (PDB ID: 4FKC).33 Automated model building was performed using phenix.autobuild.34 Subsequently, the model was completed by iterative rounds of manual model building using COOT35 and refinements using REFMAC536 and phenix.refine.34 Evaluation of the models was carried out using MolProbity.37 The coordinates, structure factors, and intensities were deposited in the PDB with IDs: 5GIQ (Dr-smAPP) and 5CNX (Ec-smAPP). Statistics describing crystallographic data collection and refinement are summarized in Table 1. Structural analyses were performed using Chimera38 and PyMol,39 and the illustrations were prepared using PyMol.

2.3 Enzyme assays
Xaa-Pro dipeptide, Xaa-Pro-Ala tripeptide, and Xaa-Pro-Pro-Gly tetrapeptide substrates were obtained from Biojoure (New Delhi, India). Arg-Pro-Pro, Arg-Pro-Pro-Gly, Arg-Pro-Pro-Gly-Phe, Arg-Pro-Pro-Gly-Phe-Ser, Arg-Pro-Pro-Gly-Phe-Ser-Pro, Met-Ala, Met-Ala-Ala, Met-Gly-Ala, Met-Ala-Pro, Met-Ser-Pro, Leu-Ser-Ala, and Leu-Ser-Ala-Ala were obtained from Sigma Chem. Co. (St. Louis, MO).

The specific activities of the purified Dr-smAPP (and its mutants), Ec-smAPP, and Mt-smAPP proteins were tested using 2.5 mM substrates in 80 μL reaction mixture containing 50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, and 1 mM MnSO4. Reaction mixtures were incubated for 10 minutes at 55°C. The reaction was stopped by adding 320 μL of alcoholic-ninhydrin reagent (prepared by mixing, 0.8 g of ninhydrin in 80 mL of ethanol and 10 mL of glacial acetic acid to which 1 g of CdCl2 dissolved in 1 mL of water was added). The resultant mixtures were boiled for 4 minutes for developing color, and the absorbance was measured at 504 nm.3 For determination of free proline in reactions with substrates Pro-Pro and Pro-Pro-Ala, the reactions were stopped by adding 80 μL each of glacial acetic acid and acidic-ninhydrin reagent (prepared by mixing 3.0 g ninhydrin in a mixture of 60 mL of glacial acetic acid and 40 mL of phosphoric acid at 70°C). The resultant mixture was boiled for 10 minutes, and absorbance was measured at 515 nm. The optimal reaction condition used for the Pf-peptidase activity was as previously reported.24 The buffer used was 50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.0, 1.2 mM CoCl2, and the reaction mixture was incubated at 97°C for 10 minutes. One unit of enzyme activity was defined as the amount of enzyme that released 1 μmole of free amino acid/proline per minute under the assay condition. The pH and temperature optima for Ec-smAPP and Pf-peptidase proteins have been reported earlier.22, 24 Those were 8.0 and 55°C for Ec-smAPP and 7.0 and 100°C for Pf-peptidase, respectively. We determined the pH and temperature optima for Dr-smAPP and Mt-smAPP proteins using Leu-Pro substrates. The pH and temperature optima for both the enzymes were found to be 8.0°C and 55°C, respectively (Supporting Information Figure S2). Activity assay was carried out at 55°C and 37°C for two substrates (Supporting Information Table S-I).

The kinetics data obtained were subjected to statistical analysis using t test. A confidence interval of 95% was used to compare the means of wild type with that of mutants.

2.4 Sequence analysis
The Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) was used for the similarity protein sequence searches through the NCBI-BLAST webpage interface (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/BLAST/).40 The multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) were carried out using Clustal-omega online server (http://www.ebi.ac.uk/Tools/msa/clustalo/).41 The MSAs of small prolidases, bacterial small aminopeptidases-P, and archaeal small aminopeptidases-P were carried out using 130, 830, and 133 sequences, respectively. The sequence logo representations of MSAs were carried out using WebLogo at server, http://weblogo.berkeley.edu/.42

3 RESULTS
3.1 Small aminopeptidase-P from E. coli
The small aminopeptidase-P from E. coli (Ec-smAPP) is a 39.6 kDa enzyme and has been enzymatically characterized as an aminopeptidase-P previously.22 We tested the activity of the enzyme toward Xaa-Pro dipeptides and Xaa-Pro-Ala tripeptides and found that it is significantly more active toward the tripeptides than the corresponding dipeptides (Figure 1A; Table 2). This preference to longer peptide substrates is typical for aminopeptidases. The crystal structure of Ec-smAPP was solved to 2.6 Å resolution (Figure 2A; Table 1). The experimental structure factors and the coordinates of the refined model have been deposited in the PDB under the accession code 5CNX. The asymmetric unit of Ec-smAPP structure contains three monomer subunits with each chain comprising 360 amino acid residues, two Zn2+ ions, and one cacodylate ion. The three chains of the asymmetric unit show Cα RMSD of 0.55 to 0.85 Å. The protein adopts a two-domain structure typical of the M24B subfamily with an N-terminal domain (residues 1-123) and a C-terminal domain (residues 124-360). The C-terminal domain, adopting a typical pita-bread-fold, houses the metal binding active site. One metal ion (ZnA) is penta-coordinated and exhibits distorted trigonal bipyramidal geometry, whereas the other (ZnB) is tetra-coordinated and exhibits a tetrahedral geometry (Figure 2G, Supporting Information Figure S3, Table 3). Metal ZnA is coordinated by O1 of cacodylate ion, Glu335 Oε2, Glu321 Oε2, His292 Nε2, and Asp223 Oδ2. Metal ZnB is coordinated by O1 of cacodylate ion, Glu335 Oε1, Asp212 Oδ1, and Asp223 Oδ1. Here, Glu335 and Asp223 act as bidentate ligands and bind to both the metals.

Ec-smAPP forms a dimer in solution as shown by size-exclusion column chromatography and dynamic light scattering (Supporting Information Figure S1). The PISA analysis of the asymmetric unit was carried out to predict the probable biological dimer from the crystal structure. The enzyme forms a closed dimer (Figure 2B). Within the three chains of asymmetric unit, the chains A and C form the first dimer whereas the second dimer is formed between the chain B and symmetry-related chain B of neighboring asymmetric unit. The subunits of first dimer of Ec-smAPP are relatively closer to each other with buried solvent accessible area of 1369 Å2 on each subunit (Figure 2C). The second dimer of Ec-smAPP is in open conformation with buried solvent accessible area of 1080 Å2 (Figure 2D). An open dimer involves interactions between N-terminal domains of both subunits and also between C-terminal domains of both subunits without any N-terminal domain to C-terminal domain interactions. N-terminal domains mainly involve main-chain interactions and Van der Waals contacts. Most of the interactions of N-terminal domain are contributed by helix α5 and the loop preceding it (Supporting Information Figure S4). Helix α5 from both subunits are perpendicular to each other and form interactions with loop regions of the other subunit. On the other hand, interactions between C-terminal domains primarily involve antiparallel interaction between helices α7 from the two subunits (Supporting Information Figure S4). These helical interactions are stabilized by hydrogen bonding between Arg172 and Glu168. In the closed dimer, we also find interactions between N-terminal domain of one subunit and the C-terminal domain of the other subunit. These correspond to dimeric interactions close to the active site and include the DXRY motif (Figure 2B,H).

3.2 Small aminopeptidase-P from D. radiodurans
A putative M24B peptidase from D. radiodurans (Dr-smAPP), 39% identical to Ec-smAPP, is a 37.1 kDa enzyme. We tested the activity of the enzyme toward Xaa-Pro dipeptides and Xaa-Pro-Ala tripeptides and found that it is significantly more active toward the tripeptides than the corresponding dipeptides (Figure 1B; Table 2). This preference to longer Xaa-Pro peptides shows that this enzyme is indeed an aminopeptidase-P. The crystal structure of Dr-smAPP was solved to 1.8 Å resolution (Figure 2A; Table 1). The experimental structure factors and the coordinates of the refined model have been deposited in the PDB under the accession code 5GIQ. The monomers of the two proteins (Ec-smAPP and Dr-smAPP) show RMSD of about 1.7 Å between their 337 Cα aligned atoms. The asymmetric unit of Dr-smAPP protein contains a single protein molecule composed of 349 amino acid residues, 2 Zn2+ ions, and 1 phosphate ion. The protein adopts a two-domain structure typical of the M24B subfamily with an N-terminal domain (residues 1-121) and a C-terminal domain (residues 122-349). The C-terminal domain, adopting a typical pita-bread-fold, houses the metal binding active site. One metal ion (ZnA) is penta-coordinated and exhibits distorted trigonal bipyramidal geometry, whereas the other (ZnB) is tetra-coordinated and exhibits a tetrahedral geometry (Figure 2G, Supporting Information Figure S3A, Table 3). Metal ZnA of Dr-smAPP is coordinated by O3 of phosphate ion, His285 Nε2, and Glu328 Oε1 in the equatorial plane and Asp221 Oδ2 and Glu314 Oε2 in the axial sites. Metal ZnB of Dr-smAPP is coordinated by O3 of phosphate ion, Asp210 Oδ1, Asp221 Oδ1, and Glu328 Oε2. Glu328 and Asp221 act as bidentate ligands and bind to both the metals. Dr-smAPP forms a dimer in solution as shown by size-exclusion column chromatography and dynamic light scattering (Supporting Information Figure S1). The PISA analysis of the asymmetric unit was carried out to predict the probable biological dimer from the crystal structure. The enzyme forms a closed dimer. The dimer of Dr-smAPP is formed by crystallography symmetry operation on an asymmetric unit comprising single chain and buries a solvent accessible area of 1090 Å2 on each monomer. This corresponds to the open dimer conformation.

3.3 Residues important for enzymatic activity
In order to test the importance of some residues close to the active site, six individual mutants (D53A, R55A, Y56A, H193A, H281A, and R298A) of Dr-smAPP were constructed. Asp53, Arg55, and Tyr56 are part of the conserved DXRY motif, which is important for enzymatic activity, His193 is expected to interact with the DXRY motif in the closed conformation and may also be involved in substrate binding, His281 is expected to be part of the proline binding pocket, and Arg298 is expected to interact with tripeptide and longer peptide substrates. The D53A, R55A, and Y56A mutants were significantly less active than the wild-type (WT) protein toward Xaa-Pro-Ala tripeptides (Figure 3). Michaelis Menten kinetics was carried out for the DXRY motif mutants using two substrates (Table 4). Although mutation in all three residues leads to lowering of k cat (P < 0.05) and increase in K m (P < 0.05), the D53A mutation causes the greatest loss in k cat for the enzyme. Thus, residues of conserved DXRY motif (Asp53, Arg55, and Tyr56) are important for the activity in Dr-smAPP. In the closed conformation of Ec-smAPP structure, Tyr55 (Tyr56 in Dr-smAPP) of DXRY motif interacts with His195 (His193 in Dr-smAPP) of PH loop (Figure 2H and Figure 3B). Mutation of His193 leads to obliteration of the activity in Dr-smAPP (Figure 3). His193 is very close to the active site metal ions and is probably involved in substrate binding. The comparison of Dr-smAPP structure with substrate bound structure of AMPP-Ec (canonical aminopeptidase-P, 50 kDa) suggest that His281 of Dr-smAPP is one of the residues that form the proline binding pocket in the active site.43 H281A mutation leads to 10-fold reduction in the activity possibly because of poor substrate binding. Arg298 is relatively away from the core active site; however, the suitable conformation of its side chain might interact with tripeptide or longer peptide substrates. Our mutagenesis result supports this hypothesis. R298A mutant exhibits 4-fold lower activity than the WT enzyme. Interestingly, both His281 and Arg298 residues were found to be disordered in the Dr-smAPP structure.

3.4 Small aminopeptidase-P from M. tuberculosis
Small aminopeptidase-P is conserved in M. tuberculosis which is significantly diverged from E. coli and D. radiodurans. The putative small aminopeptidase-P from M. tuberculosis (Mt-smAPP) is a 38.7 kDa enzyme. It shares 35% sequence identity with Ec-smAPP and 39% sequence identity with Dr-smAPP. We tested the activity of Mt-smAPP toward Xaa-Pro dipeptides and Xaa-Pro-Ala tripeptides and found that this enzyme is also significantly more active toward the tripeptides than the corresponding dipeptides (Figure 1C; Table 2). This confirms the identity of the enzyme as a small aminopeptidase-P.

3.5 Structural comparison of Dr-smAPP with canonical aminopeptidase
Because the activity of Dr-smAPP and Ec-smAPP classifies them as APP, we compared the structure of Dr-smAPP with AMPP-Ec, the canonical aminopeptidase P from E. coli.18 The two proteins share about 35% sequence identity between their C-terminal domains and virtually no sequence identity between their N-terminal domains. The C-terminal domains of the two proteins overlap fairly well with each other (Figure 4A) with RMSD of 1.45 Å with 217 aligned Cα atoms. Metal binding active site is well-conserved between the two proteins. In contrast, the N-terminal domains of the two proteins have diverged from each other showing RMSD of 2.5 Å with 107 aligned Cα atoms. N-terminal domains from these two proteins have some prominent differences. AMPP-Ec has two conspicuous protruding loops in the N-terminal domain that are absent in Dr-smAPP (Figure 4A). The first loop corresponds to a 14 residues insertion between strand β1 and helix α2 of Dr-smAPP (Supporting Information Figure S5). Majority of the loop lacks regular secondary structure; however, it does form two short interacting β-strands toward the tip of the loop region. These loops are involved in the dimerization of AMPP-Ec structure. The other protruding loop corresponds to a 10 residues insertion after strand β3 of Dr-smAPP and houses a short helical section. This elongated loop of AMPP-Ec interacts with the loop in the active site of the other subunit. Because of difference in orientation of the dimers, even the smaller corresponding region of Dr-smAPP which houses the DXRY motif interacts with PH loop of the other subunit. The polypeptides of small aminopeptidases-P are smaller than that of AMPP-Ec primarily because of absence of these two protruding loops. The absence of these loops places centroids of the N-terminal domains from two subunits much closer to each other in Dr-smAPP than that of AMPP-Ec. Further, helix α5 of Dr-smAPP is shorter than the corresponding helix in AMPP-Ec (Figure 4A). This helix of AMPP-Ec is involved in the tetramerization interface of the protein. In absence of this structural feature, the Dr-smAPP protein does not form the higher order oligomer.

3.6 Structural comparison of Dr-smAPP with prolidase
The closest structural homologs of Dr-smAPP are archaeal and bacterial prolidases (PDB IDs: 5FCF, 1WN1 and 4ZNG).23, 45, 46 We compared the Dr-smAPP structure with that of the small prolidase from Xanthomonas campestris (PDB ID: 5FCF).23 The superposition of their N-domains shows an RMSD of 2.1 Å with 120 aligned Cα atoms whereas superposition of their C-domains shows RMSD of 1.4 Å with 217 aligned Cα atoms. The only noticeable difference between the structures is the presence of loop comprising XER motif in the prolidase (Figure 4B) corresponding to insertion of three residues (SER; 70-72) before strand β2 of Dr-smAPP. This loop of the N-terminal domain interacts with the active site region of the C-terminal domain of the other subunit of a dimer. The Arg72 of this loop interacts with free α-carboxylate group of dipeptide substrate and plays an important role in dipeptide selectivity of the small prolidase. Absence of this loop in small aminopeptidases-P enables these enzymes to accommodate substrates longer than dipeptide.

3.7 Peptidase from P. furiosus
Structural features including absence of XER motif containing loop and also of conserved Arg residue were observed in M24B peptidase from P. furiosus. This enzyme was previously reported as a prolidase.25 We tested the activity of the enzyme toward Xaa-Pro dipeptides and Xaa-Pro-Ala tripeptides and found that it is significantly more active toward the tripeptides than the corresponding dipeptides (Figure 1D; Table 2). This preference to longer Xaa-Pro peptides shows that, unlike its previous classification, this enzyme is actually an aminopeptidase-P.

3.8 Enzymatic activities toward other substrates
Apart from the Xaa-Pro and Xaa-Pro-Ala substrates mentioned earlier, the activity of the small-aminopeptidases-P was tested toward few other substrates (Supporting Information Figure S6). The ability of these enzymes to process Phe-Pro-His and Arg-Pro-Pro substrates apart from the Xaa-Pro-Ala substrates shows that the P2’ pocket of these enzymes can accommodate residues of varying sizes. The enzymes were found to process bradykinin-derived substrates (Xaa-Pro-Pro-Gly-) with reasonable efficiency. The enzymes were also found to process other substrates that have residues other than Pro at P1’ position. Met/Leu-Ala/Gly/Ser-Xaa- substrates were tested. Activities toward these substrates were in general much lower than those for the substrates with Pro at the P1’ position. This type of substrate specificity is typical for M24B peptidases.

4 DISCUSSION
4.1 Typical features of small aminopeptidases-P
Earlier, a distinct class of aminopeptidases-P (small aminopeptidases-P; MW ~36-39 kDa) were purified and enzymatically characterized from E. coli and other bacteria. Sequence analysis shows that these proteins are diverged from canonical AMPP-Ec but closer to small-prolidases. Crystal structures indeed reveal that AMPP-Ec has additional protruding loops in its N-terminal domain, which contribute toward differences in their monomeric structure and in their dimeric organization. Our structural studies show that both monomeric and dimeric organizations of small aminopeptidases-P are almost identical to those of small prolidases. The only noticeable difference between them is absence of the loop comprising residues of XER motif in small-aminopeptidases-P (Figure 4B). This loop of small prolidases houses an Arg residue (Arg72 in small prolidase from Xanthomonas campestris) that is responsible for the dipeptide selectivity.23 The absence of this dipeptide selectivity loop in the N-terminal domain of small aminopeptidases-P enables them to hydrolyze longer peptides.

4.2 Canonical prolidase is in fact aminopeptidase-P
Analysis of MSA of small prolidases shows that XER motif is highly conserved (Figure 5A).23, 24 Moreover, the analysis reveals a highly conserved HRXGH motif (residues 327HRTGH331 in small prolidase from Xanthomonas campestris) in the C-terminal domain of small prolidases. The conserved Arg residue (Arg293 in Lactococcus lactis) of this motif was earlier shown to be important for the enzymatic activity of small prolidases.47 We noticed that this Arg is absent in small aminopeptidases-P (Figure 5B) whereas rest of the motif is still conserved. Interestingly, we also noticed that this critical Arg is absent in the canonical archaeal prolidase from P. furiosus (Pf-peptidase; PDB ID: 1PV9) (Figure 5C).24, 25 This was the first structurally characterized enzyme that was reported as a prolidase and has been well cited in literature. The structure of Pf-peptidase matches very well with that of Dr-smAPP, especially as both proteins lack dipeptide selectivity loop containing the XER motif (Figure 6). This raises doubts that Pf-peptidase could be a small aminopeptidases-P. We examined this enzyme for aminopeptidase-P activity by using substrates with peptide length longer than dipeptides. We found that Pf-peptidase cleaves tripeptides and longer peptides. Hence, this enzyme is an aminopeptidase-P (Figure 1D). Earlier, Pf-peptidase was assigned as prolidase based on its inability to cleave longer peptide substrates. This may have been because of poor choice of substrates.24 Our success might have been because of the enzymatic assays with extensive set of Xaa-Pro-Ala and bradykinin-based substrates. In fact, Pf-peptidase was found to be much more efficient at cleaving longer peptides than some of the other small aminopeptidases-P enzymes we tested.

4.3 Distinguishing small aminopeptidases-P from other M24B peptidases
Zheng et al. identified DXRY sequence motif in the N-terminal region of small aminopeptidase-P from E. coli (Ec-smAPP) and its homologs.22 This motif could potentially identify small aminopeptidases-P from the closely related M24B peptidases. However, the function of the residues of this motif was not known. Our structure of Ec-smAPP revealed the proximity of this motif to the active site, especially in the closed conformation of the enzyme (Figure 2E). This fact, along with the widespread conservation of the motif, suggests that the residues of this motif must be important for the activity of the small aminopeptidases-P. This was confirmed by our site-directed mutagenesis studies in Dr-smAPP. Mutations D53A, R55A, and Y56A led to considerable loss in activity of Dr-smAPP enzyme (Figure 3A). Indeed, our study shows that all three selected proteins from evolutionarily diverged bacterial species with DXRY motif are Aminopeptidases-P. Thus, the DXRY motif can be useful in distinguishing small-aminopeptidases-P from other closely related enzymes of the M24B family, especially small-prolidases. However, it is not a necessary criterion for identifying small aminopeptidases-P. Although most bacterial small aminopeptidases-P have the DXRY motif, most archaeal small aminopeptidases-P lack this motif (Figure 5B,C). Pf-peptidase, which we have characterized as small-aminopeptidase-P in this study, is one such archaeal enzyme. Thus, absence of substrate selectivity loop comprising XER motif (in N-terminal domain) and absence of conserved Arg in HRXGH motif (in C-terminal domain) can be a good indicator for identifying small aminopeptidases-P from closely related M24B peptidases.

Interestingly, two prolidases (PH1149 and PH0974) were earlier reported from P. horikossi, a species closely related to P. furiosus.48 The crystal structures of these archaeal M24B peptidases were also reported (PDB IDs: 1WY2 and 1WN1, respectively). Based on the present studies, we propose that one of these peptidases, which was annotated as prolidase (gene ID, PH1149; UniProt accession ID, O58885; PDB ID: 1WY2), is a small aminopeptidase-P. The other peptidase (gene ID, PH0974; UniProt accession ID, O58691; PDB ID: 1WN1) is a genuine prolidase of small-prolidase type, which has a substrate selectivity loop comprising XER motif. Further, our analysis indicates that the structure of M24B peptidase from Bacillus anthracis (PDB ID: 3Q6D), which was annotated as a prolidase is also a small aminopeptidase-P. Thus, our present study provides important information for correctly identifying the M24B peptidases as prolidases or aminopeptidases-P.

4.4 Conservation and importance of DXRY motif
Our sequence analyses show that the conserved DXRY sequence motif is found not only in bacterial small aminopeptidases-P but also in the N-terminal domains of eukaryotic three-domain aminopeptidases-P including those of human XPNPEP1, human XPNPEP2, and APP from C. elegans (Figure 7A). In spite of lack of sequence identity between them, N-terminal domains of bacterial small aminopeptidases-P superpose very well with N-terminal domains of three-domain eukaryotic aminopeptidases-P most notably in the DXRY loop regions (Figure 7B). The N-terminal domains of Dr-smAPP and XPNPEP1 superpose with RMSD of 1.9 Å between the 119 aligned Cα atoms. Further structural comparison of Dr-smAPP dimer with that of XPNPEP1 monomer shows that the N-terminal domain of three-domain XPNPEP1 protein is equivalent to the N-terminal domain of the other subunit in an Dr-smAPP dimer (Figure 7C,D). Based on these observations, it appears that XPNPEP1 has evolved from a small-aminopeptidases-P-like protein via duplication of its N-terminal domain thus forming the three-domain protein of XPNPEP1. During the course of evolution, it has lost the residues of the DXRY sequence motif in the middle domain whereas retaining them in the N-terminal domain of XPNPEP1. The structural features of dimeric interactions involving N-terminal domains of Dr-smAPP are also similar to those seen in the interaction of middle-domain and N-terminal domain of XPNPEP1 (Figure 7E). Further, we show that Dr-smAPP, like XPNPEP1 and XPNPEP2, efficiently cleaves the bradykinin-based peptide substrates (Supporting Information Figure S6A).50 These observations support the idea of common evolutionary origin of bacterial small aminopeptidases-P and three-domain eukaryotic aminopeptidases-P.

Our mutation data clearly shows that the residues of DXRY motif are important for the enzymatic activity of Dr-smAPP (Figure 3A). We also mutated His193 of Dr-smAPP, an active site residue proximal to DXRY motif. Mutation of this residue to Ala completely abolished the enzymatic activity. This His193 mutagenesis result is consistent with the earlier reports about equivalent His residue in AMPP-Ec.43 To illuminate the structural role of the residues of DXRY motif we compared the Dr-smAPP structure with structure of apstatin bound three-domain APP from C. elegans (Figure 7F). We found that the residues of DXRY motif aligned very well between the two proteins (Figure 7A,B). The role of the Asp, Arg, and Tyr residues can be deduced form this structural comparison. The Arg residue binds to the carbonyl oxygen of P1’ proline of the peptide substrate. The Asp residue stabilizes the appropriate side chain conformation of the Arg residue in the DXRY motif. The Tyr residue interacts with the His residue of the PH loop and stabilizes its side chain conformation. Earlier the role of equivalent His residue (His243) in AMPP-Ec was proposed for the substrate binding, more specifically binding to the carbonyl oxygen of P1’ residue of peptide substrate.43 We propose that His193 plays a similar role in Dr-smAPP.

In conclusion, our study provides sequence and structural features that resolve the ambiguity in annotation of widely conserved small prokaryotic prolidases and small aminopeptidases-P. We show experimental evidence that a widely cited canonical prolidase (Pf-peptidase) is in fact a small aminopeptidase-P. Further, we propose an evolutionary link between small prokaryotic aminopeptidase P and large three-domain aminopeptidase P from eukaryotes. Our structural and mutagenesis studies also illuminate the roles of several active site residues in small aminopeptidases-P.

Crystal structure and functional assignment of YfaU, a metal ion dependent class II aldolase from Escherichia coli K12

Abstract
One of the major challenges in the postgenomic era is the functional assignment of proteins using sequence- and structure-based predictive methods coupled with experimental validation. We have used these approaches to investigate the structure and function of the Escherichia coli K-12 protein YfaU, annotated as a putative 4-hydroxy-2-ketoheptane-1,7-dioate aldolase (HpcH) in the sequence databases. HpcH is the final enzyme in the degradation pathway of the aromatic compound homoprotocatechuate. We have determined the crystal structure of apo-YfaU and the Mg2+−pyruvate product complex. Despite greater sequence and structural similarity to HpcH, genomic context suggests YfaU is instead a 2-keto-3-deoxy sugar aldolase like the homologous 2-dehydro-3-deoxygalactarate aldolase (DDGA). Enzyme kinetic measurements show activity with the probable physiological substrate 2-keto-3-deoxy-l-rhamnonate, supporting the functional assignment, as well as the structurally similar 2-keto-3-deoxy-l-mannonate and 2-keto-3-deoxy-l-lyxonate (see accompanying paper: Rakus, J. F., Fedorov, A. A., Fedorov, E. V., Glasner, M. E., Hubbard, B. K., Delli, J. D., Babbitt, P. C., Almo, S. C., and Gerlt, J. A. (2008) Biochemistry47, 9944−9954). YfaU has similar activity toward the HpcH substrate 4-hydroxy-2-ketoheptane-1,7-dioate and synthetic substrates 4-hydroxy-2-ketopentanoic acid and 4-hydroxy-2-ketohexanoic acid. This indicates a relaxed substrate specificity that complicates the functional assignment of members of this enzyme superfamily. Crystal structures suggest these enzymes use an Asp-His intersubunit dyad to activate a metal-bound water or hydroxide for proton transfer during catalysis.

Functional annotation of genomes presents a major challenge for biology in the 21st century (1, 2). Although the function of some gene products can be predicted by sequence comparison with well-studied homologues, the functions of many others remain unknown (3). Between these groups lie genes whose functional designation is susceptible to misinterpretation as a result of incorrect or misleading comparison to other genes. It is long established that proteins with highly related sequences can perform different functions in vivo, and conversely many proteins have similar functions despite sharing little or no sequence similarity. Structural comparisons of proteins can provide important functional clues since structure is more conserved through evolution than sequence. Structural genomics initiatives are providing an ever-expanding database of protein structural information that provides a valuable resource for functional genome annotation (4, 5). However, greater effort is required if incomplete or incorrect functional annotation is to be avoided. Recent reports in the literature highlight the power of combining computational and experimental approaches for functional annotation (6, 7). In these studies virtual ligand screening and docking using experimentally determined and modeled structures were used to identify potential substrates. Experimental validation of the substrates and determination of the enzyme−ligand complexes confirmed the correct identification of the substrates and provided justification for this approach to functional annotation.
Aromatic degradative pathways utilize a diverse array of enzymatic activities that may be appropriate for use in synthetic chemistry for the stereoselective synthesis of organic compounds. Research in this area may facilitate the development of biodegradable or biotechnologically useful chemicals and engineered enzymes or organisms useful for bioremediation (8, 9). One of the longest characterized aromatic degradative pathways involves the catabolism of 4-hydroxyphenylacetate (4-HPA1), which is converted to 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetate or homoprotocatechuate (HPC) and subsequently degraded by a series of enzymes to the central metabolites pyruvate and succinic semialdehyde (10, 11). 4-HPA degradation pathway genes are present in a wide range of bacteria, and homologues of these genes are present in many other organisms including higher eukaryotes. HpcH catalyzes the final step in this pathway, the retro-aldol conversion of 4-hydroxy-2-ketoheptane-1,7-dioate to pyruvate and succinic semialdehyde (12, 13). HpcH is a divalent metal ion dependent class II aldolase belonging to the pyruvate/enolpyruvate-binding (β/α)8 barrel superfamily. The K12 strain of Escherichia coli does not contain the HPC pathway genes and is consequently incapable of utilizing 4-HPA as a sole carbon source. It is therefore surprising to find a gene in E. coli K12 (gene b2245) encoding YfaU (GI: 18206229), a protein which is 53% identical to HpcH (Figure 1) and is annotated as a putative 4-hydroxy-2-ketoheptane-1,7-dioate aldolase in the sequence databases. The next closest sequence homologue of YfaU is the E. coli K12 enzyme 2-dehydro-3-deoxygalactarate aldolase (DDGA, 43% sequence identity). Sequence identity alone therefore suggests YfaU is a putative aldolase involved in aromatic degradation. To investigate the function of YfaU, and to further investigate the structure−function and evolutionary relationships of this biotechnologically important class of enzymes, we have determined the crystal structures of apo-YfaU to 1.39 Å resolution and a Mg2+−pyruvate product complex to 1.93 Å resolution. The structure is typical of the (β/α)8 barrel superfamily of divalent metal ion dependent class II aldolases. Of particular note is the Asp-His intersubunit dyad that appears to activate a metal-bound water or hydroxide for proton transfer during catalysis.
