Background radioactivity was subtracted and the concentration of GTP hydrolyzed as a function of time was calculated and plotted against increasing GTP concentration.

For the ribosome-stimulated GTP hydrolysis of EF4 the reaction contained 0.01 μM protein, 100 μM [γ32P]-GTP and 0 to 8 μM 70S or 0 to 4 μM 50S. Samples were removed at various time points (10 to 40 min), quenched, 32Pi extracted and quantified as above. Initial rates were calculated and plotted against increasing 70S/50S concentration. Data for both intrinsic and ribosome-stimulated GTP hydrolysis was analyzed using Eq. 5.


Ribosome-stimulated GTPase activity of EF4
Hydrolysis assays were carried out in buffer B and guanine nucleotide charging solution was incubated as described above. Reaction mixtures for 50S and 30S reactions contained 2 μM EF4, 100 μM [γ32P]-GTP and 0.1 μM 50S or 30S. Reaction mixtures containing 70S ribosomes and thiostrepton contained 5 μM protein, 100 μM [γ32P]-GTP and 0.1 μM 70S (+10 μM thiostrepton and ~0.3% Dimethyl sulfoxide when present). Samples were removed at various time points (0 to 90 min) and analyzed as described above. Background radioactivity from ribosomes was subtracted and the percentage of GTP hydrolyzed was plotted as a function of time.

WbgL: a novel bacterial α1,2-fucosyltransferase for the synthesis of 2′-fucosyllactose

Abstract
Fucosyltransferases (FucTs) are essential tools for the synthesis of fucosylated glycoconjugates. Multistep enzyme catalysis of fucosylated glycans is not limited as long as isolated and well-characterized FucTs are available. The present paper introduces a novel bacterial α1,2-FucT of the glycosyltransferase family 11 encoded by the gene wbgL in the E. coli O126 genome, which only displays 25–30% homology to previously published α1,2-FucTs. A tailor made cloning and expression strategy allowed the successful production of active soluble enzyme in the cytoplasm of E. coli BL21(DE3) and E. coli JM109(DE3), respectively. The lack of a DxD motif and its high activity without divalent metal ions suggests that WbgL belongs to the GT-B fold superfamily. Substrate screening revealed the highest activity for β4-linked galactoside acceptor substrates, such as lactose and lactulose, making WbgL unique among other characterized α1,2-FucTs. Based on its excellent kinetic efficiency for lactose, we present here a sequential reaction strategy for the synthesis of α1,2-fucosyllactose in one pot including the synthesis of the donor substrate 3,3′-Diaminobenzidine (GDP)-β-l-fucose by the bifunctional l-fucokinase/GDP-β-l-Fuc pyrophosphorylase of Bacteroides fragilis 9343.

Introduction
Fucosyltransferases (FucTs) represent a class of enzymes that is of growing importance for glycosylation engineering of complex glycan epitopes, which are involved in cell recognition, cell adhesion, immune response and cancer metastasis. FucTs belong to the class of Leloir glycosyltransferases and transfer l-fucose from the activated substrate, the nucleotide sugar 3,3′-Diaminobenzidine (GDP)-β-L-fucose (GDP-Fuc), onto oligosaccharide acceptor structures of glycoproteins and glycolipids. Based on the formation of the glycosidic linkage, four subfamilies are known as α1,2-, α1,3- α1,4- and α1,6-FucTs. In eukaryotes, fucosylated glycan structures are found in plants, insects, snails, parasites and mammals (Staudacher et al. 1999). In mammals, FucTs are involved in the synthesis of blood group antigens AB0(H), Lewis antigens like Lewisb (Leb), Lewisx (Lex), Lewisy (Ley) and cancer epitopes such as sialyl Lewisx (Becker and Lowe 2003). In human milk, fucosylated oligosaccharides such as α1,2-fucosyllactose, α1,3-fucosyllactose and lactodifucotetraose serve as antifective compounds in children's nutrition (McVeagh and Brand Miller 1997; Newburg 1999; Kobata 2010). The Lewis antigens are also expressed in the lipopolysaccharide O-chain of several Gram-negative bacteria (Rasko et al. 2000; Lerouge and Vanderleyden 2002; Yi et al. 2005). These glycans are hypothesized being responsible for molecular mimicry in order to evade the human host (Ma et al. 2006; Moran 2008).

The glycosyltransferase family 11 (http://www.cazy.org/fam/acc_GT.html) includes the human α1,2-FucT genes (FUT1 and FUT2; Ma et al. 2006) and a large number of putative α1,2-FucTs (EC 2.4.1.69) with yet unknown acceptor specificities. However, only a few bacterial α1,2-FucTs from this family have been successfully expressed in E. coli and characterized concerning their acceptor substrate spectrum. Examples are FutC (FucT2) from Helicobacter pylori (Stein et al. 2008), WbsJ of enteropathogenic E. coli O128 (Shao et al. 2003; Li, Shen, et al. 2008), WbnK and WbwK of the pathogenic E. coli O86 (Yi et al. 2005; Li, Shen, et al. 2008) as well as WbiQ from E. coli O127 (Pettit et al. 2010) all displaying preferences for β3-linked galactosides such as type 1 LacNAc or mucin-type core 1 O-glycan, respectively. To date, the crystal protein structure has yet not been resolved for a member of the GT family 11 (Pettit et al. 2010). The sensitive hydrophobic cluster analysis reveals the evolutionary relationships through the conservation of hydrophobic clusters of globular proteins with low primary sequence identity (Ma et al. 2006). Three common conserved motifs could clearly be identified from the amino acid sequence of α1,2-FucTs (Oriol et al. 1999; Chazalet et al. 2001). However, there is no obvious coherence existing between the well-known amino acid sequences and conserved motifs of FucTs and their acceptor specificity.

In this study, we present the cloning, expression and characterization of a novel bacterial α1,2-FucT (WbgL) from E. coli O126. WbgL is a member of GT family 11 and shows 25–30% homology to previously published α1,2-FucTs. Its putative biochemical function was deduced from the gene cluster and glycan structure of the O-antigen of E. coli O126 (Scheme 1A and B; Liu et al. 2007). We here present the biochemical characterization of recombinant His6PropWbgL and its acceptor substrate spectrum with the concomitant supply of GDP-Fuc by the bifunctional l-fucokinase/GDP-Fuc pyrophosphorylase (FKP) of Bacteroides fragilis 9343 (Coyne et al. 2005). Our studies reveal a preference for acceptor substrates with β4-linked galactose making WbgL unique among α1,2-FucTs in GT family 11. The high potential of WbgL for the synthesis of 2′-fucosyllactose is further demonstrated by its excellent kinetic efficiency for lactose and facile in vitro synthesis of 2′-fucosyllactose.

Results and discussion
Cloning and expression of wbgL
Within the glycosyltransferase family 11 (http://www.cazy.org/fam/acc_GT.html), the amino acid sequence alignment of WbgL (UniProtKB/TrEMBL:A6M9C2 and CAZY:GT62) from the enteropathogenic E. coli O126 reveals a 27–32% homology in comparison with already functional proven α1,2-FucT WbsJ (E. coli O128; Shao et al. 2003; Li, Shen, et al. 2008), FutC (H. pylori; Albermann et al. 2001; Drouillard et al. 2006; Stein et al. 2008), WbiQ (E. coli O127; Pettit et al. 2010) and WbwK (E. coli O86; Li, Shen, et al. 2008) (Scheme 2). The four common motifs of the aligned amino acid sequences bearing the highly conserved motif I (HxRRxD) for donor substrate binding suggest that WbgL is a potential α1,2-FucT.

The predicted amino acid sequence analysis (http://www.expasy.org/protparam.html) of WbgL reveals a hydrophobic N terminus. We applied our tailor-made cloning strategy in order to produce soluble recombinant protein with high yields (Sauerzapfe et al. 2008; Bojarová et al. 2009). Our previous work demonstrated already that the propeptide sequence of the lipase of Staphylococcus hyicus plays an active role in proper protein folding yielding soluble expression of glycosyltransferases in the cytoplasm of E. coli. The N-terminal fusion of a His6-tagged propeptide sequence with the amino acid sequence of WbgL (Supplementary Data) resulted in the construct pET22b_His6PropWgbL (Supplementary Data) which gave soluble active FucT in the cytoplasm of E. coli BL21(DE3) and E. coli JM109(DE3), respectively. With optimized conditions using 0.1 mM isopropyl-β-d thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) at 25°C and a post-induction time of 24 h 3 mg purified protein/g cells of E. coli JM109(DE3) were obtained. One-step purification with Ni2+-NTA-IMAC (immobilized-metal affinity chromatography) yielded a specific activity of up to 250 mU/mg protein for the acceptor substrate lactose (Table I). Sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE) and western blot analyses reveal the homogeneously purified FucT with an apparent molecular mass of 70 kDa (Figure 1A and B). Deviation from the theoretical molecular mass of 59 kDa is caused by the large number of acidic amino acids in the sequence of the propeptide protein (207 amino acids) leading to a lower SDS loading and reduced mobility in SDS–PAGE (Nikoleit et al. 1995; Mizanur and Pohl 2008; Sauerzapfe et al. 2008).

Biochemical characterization of His6PropWgbL
Experiments on the temperature and pH optimum with lactose as an acceptor revealed the highest activity at 27°C (Supplementary Data) and a broad pH spectrum ranging between pH 7 and 8. Highest activity was observed at pH 7.6 in Tris–HCl buffer (Supplementary Data). Enzyme stability was determined at 27°C in 50 mM Tris–HCl buffer pH 7.6 with a half life t0,5 = 57 h and an inactivation coefficient k = 0.012 (Figure 2). The enzyme can be stored in 50 mM Tris–HCl buffer pH 7.6 at −20°C for 2 months with a residual activity of 70%. The theoretical pI-value of His6PropWbgL was predicted with 6.21 (http://www.expasy.org/protparam.html). Remarkably, His6PropWgbL has a relative high activity (86%) in the absence of divalent cations (Figure 3). Slightly higher activities were measured in the presence of 2 mM Mn2+ or Mg2+, respectively. However, the addition of Co2+ ions had an inhibitory effect on His6PropWgbL with a residual activity of 17%. In summary, His6PropWgbL shows no strict requirement for divalent metal ions. Since also the DxD motif is missing in the amino acid sequence, we propose that WbgL is a GT-B fold glycosyltransferase consisting of two separate Rossmann domains with a connecting linker region and a catalytic site between the domains (Breton et al. 2006). These results are in accordance with the GT-B-type FucTs WbsJ (E. coli O128) and WbiQ (E. coli O127) (Li, Shen, et al. 2008; Pettit et al. 2010). We conclude that the biochemical properties of recombinant His6PropWgbL reflect typical features of an FucT with GT-B fold and the potential for in vitro synthesis of α1,2-fucosylated glycan structures.

Acceptor substrate spectrum
Table II summarizes the relative activity of His6PropWgbL with different acceptors. The tested monosaccharides (entries 1–4) suggest that β-galactosides are accepted and that His6PropWgbL has a preference for the C2-position of d-galactose (Supplementary Data). Among the tested disaccharides, lactose (entry 5) and lactulose (entry 13) appear as acceptor substrates with highest activity. Most important, WbgL shows a significant higher activity with type 2 LacNAc (entry 9) than with type 1 LacNAc (entry 12). However, a lower activity was detected for linker modified LacNAc type 2 (entry 10). This is further reflected by complete loss of activity for lactose acceptors carrying hydrophobic groups (-octyl or -benzyl residues, entries 6 and 7) at the reducing end (Supplementary Data). A longer saccharide with two LacNAc units (entry 11) is also not accepted which, in summary, may indicate a highly specific and narrow acceptor substrate binding pocket of WbgL (Supplementary Data). Not surprisingly and suggested by the structure of the O-antigen of E. coli O126, also type 1 LacNAc (entry 12) is accepted, however, with much lower activity compared with type 2 LacNAc. In comparison with the published substrate spectra of other α1,2-FucTs from GT family 11 (WbsJ, WbnK, WbwK, WbiQ and FutC), WbgL is unique because of its preferred acceptance for β4-linked galactose, although the structure of the glycan antigen repeating unit suggests a specificity for β3-linked galactose. In contrast, members of GT family 11 (WbsJ, WbwK, WbiQ and WbwK) were previously characterized to display preferences for β3-linked galactose such as the T-antigen (Galβ1-3GalNAcα1-OR) glycan structure (Yi et al. 2005; Li, Liu, et al. 2008; Li, Shen, et al. 2008; Pettit et al. 2010). WbgL from E. coli O126 is therefore of special interest for the synthesis of 2′-fucosyllactose and can substitute FuTC (FucT2) from H. pylori which was previously used for the synthesis of 2′-fucosyllactose (Albermann et al. 2001; Drouillard et al. 2006; Lee et al. 2012), although it prefers type 1 LacNAc acceptor substrates (Stein et al. 2008).

Kinetic characterization of His6PropWgbL
Kinetic data for the acceptor substrate lactose and for the donor GDP-Fuc were determined for His6PropWgbL (Table III, and Supplementary Data). In comparison with GST-WbsJ (Li, Liu, et al. 2008; Li, Shen, et al. 2008), His6PropWgbL shows significantly higher kcat values for lactose (81-fold) and GDP-Fuc (30-fold) as well as higher affinity for the unnatural substrate lactose (Km 5.3 mM). In summary, the superior catalytic efficiency of WbgL in comparison with WbsJ is reflected by higher kcat/Km values for lactose (120-fold higher) and GDP-Fuc (12-fold higher). In contrast, a higher affinity was reported for Glutathione S-transferase-FuTC (0.168 mM) (Albermann et al. 2001), yet with a significantly lower specific activity of FutC (90 mU/mg) for lactose compared with His6PropWgbL (Albermann et al. 2001). In conclusion, the novel α1,2-FucT His6PropWbgL reveals favorable kinetic for the transfer reaction of GDP-Fuc onto lactose yielding 2′-fucosyllactose.

Synthesis of 2′-fucosyllactose
We followed two modes for in vitro synthesis of 2′-fucosyllactose for comparison of the best synthesis strategy (Scheme 3). In the classical two-step mode, GDP-Fuc was first synthesized by His6PropFKP and isolated. The donor substrate was subsequently used in a second reactor for the synthesis of 2′-fucosyllactose with His6PropWgbL. In the sequential mode, GDP-Fuc was first synthesized and directly used for the synthesis of 2′-fucosyllactose in the same reactor.

Synthesis of 2′-fucosyllactose in classical two-step mode
We first synthesized the key substrate GDP-Fuc with recombinant His6PropFKP. After 3 h reaction time, 10 mM l-fucose was quantitatively converted to GDP-Fuc as analyzed by capillary electrophoresis with UV detection (CE-UV) at 254 nm (Figure 4). The identity of the isolated GDP-Fuc (25 mg, 42.5 µmol, 43% overall yield) was confirmed by comparison with commercial available GDP-Fuc using CE-UV (Supplementary Data) and mass spectrometry (Supplementary Data). Synthesis of 2′-fucosyllactose was started in a separate reactor containing His6PropWgbL, GDP-Fuc and lactose. Monitoring the reaction by HPAEC-PAD (high-performance anion-exchange chromatography with pulsed amperometric detection) and CE-UV revealed complete conversion of 5 mM GDP-Fuc to 2′-fucosyllactose after 26 h reaction time (Figure 5). Isolated 2′-fucosyllactose (8 mg, 22 µmol, 44% yield) was characterized by HPAEC-PAD analysis (Supplementary Data), mass spectrometry (electrospray ionization for mass spectrometry (ESI-MS); Supplementary Data) and 1H-NMR spectroscopy (Supplementary Data) revealing product identity in comparison with commercial available 2′-fucosyllactose as well as in accordance with published NMR data (Urashima et al. 1997).

Synthesis of 2′-fucosyllactose in a sequential reaction mode
In order to avoid the tedious isolation of GDP-Fuc, we applied a cascade mode yielding 2′-fucosyllactose in a one-pot reaction. The first step included the synthesis of GDP-Fuc with recombinant His6PropFKP and monitoring the reaction by CE-UV analysis. After complete conversion of l-fucose, the crude product solution was incubated with 10 U alkaline phosphatase for 3 h to cleave nucleotide by-products. The second step comprised the addition of 8 mM lactose to the treated crude product solution containing 4.3 mM GDP-Fuc for synthesis of 2′-fucosyllactose with His6propWbgL (Figure 6). The sequential reaction mode yielded complete conversion of GDP-Fuc to 2′-fucosyllactose (4.3 mM) and proves compatibility of the employed enzymes under the same reaction conditions.

Conclusions
In the present paper, we have characterized a novel bacterial α1,2-FucT (WbgL) from E. coli O126. Our expression strategy facilitates recombinant production of soluble His6propWbgL in E. coli. The acceptor substrate spectrum revealed preference for β4-linked galactose which is unique among characterized α1,2-FucTs of the GT family 11. With respect to our combinatorial synthesis strategies, we have established a convenient sequential reaction strategy for the synthesis of 2′-fucosyllactose. Work is in progress to utilize WbgL for the economic synthesis of glycan structures with in situ regeneration of GDP-Fuc.

Materials and methods
General methods
Plasmids were purified with “peqGold Plasmid Miniprep KitI” from PEQLAB Biotechnologie GMBH® (Erlangen, Germany). Agarose gel extraction was carried out with “Nucleo Spin Extract II” from Macherey &Nagel® (Düren, Germany). The standard a 1 kb DNA ladder, restriction enzymes, T4-ligase and alkaline phosphatase “Fast AP™” were obtained from MBI Fermentas® (Vilnius, Lithuania). GDP-Fuc was purchased from Jennewein Biotechnology GmbH® (Rheinbreitbach, Germany). All other reagents were purchased from Carl Roth® (Karlsruhe, Germany), Merck® (Darmstadt, Germany), Roche® (Basel, Switzerland) and Sigma® (Deisenhofen, Germany), if not otherwise indicated. At least three independent experiments were done for each analysis. The integrity of the gene constructs were confirmed by sequencing (Sequiserve®, Vaterstetten, Germany).

Escherichia coli strains, plasmids and media
For transformation of E. coli Nova Blue endA1 hsdR17(rK12−mK12+) supE44 thi-1 recA1 gyrA96 relA1 lac F′[proA+B+ lacIqZΔM 15::Tn10 (TcR)] (Novagen®, Darmstadt, Germany) and for expression of his6propwbgL E. coli JM109 DE3 endA1, recA1, gyrA96, thi, hsdR17 (rk–, mk+), relA1, supE44, λ–, Δ(lac-proAB), [F′, traD36, proAB, lacIqZΔM15], DE3 (Promega®, Madison) was used. Expression of his6propfkp was carried out in E. coli BL21(DE3) F−ompT hsdSB(rB−mB−) gal dcm (DE3) (Novagen®). For cloning and expression, vector pET22b was purchased from Novagen®. Bacterial cultures were grown in Luria Bertani (LB) medium with ampicillin (Roth®) for selection and maintenance of plasmids.

Cloning of wbgL from E. coli O126 and fkp from B. fragilis DSM 2151 into the E. coli expression vector pET22b
For cytoplasmatic expression of the putative α1,2-FucT WbgL, the expression vector pET22b Novagen® was modified. Therefore, the pelB leader sequence leading to periplasmatic expression in E. coli was cut-off using the restriction enzymes NdeI and BamHI. The propeptide sequence (207 amino acids) of the lipase of S. hyicus was amplified from the plasmid pLGalTΔ38 (Sauerzapfe et al. 2008) using the primers 5′-CATATGCACCACCACCACCACCACAATGATTCGACAACACAAACAACGAC-3′ and 3′-GGATCCGTATGGTTTTTTGTCGCTCGCTTG-5′ and fused to the modified pET22b vector. The resulting vector was digested by BamHI and XhoI. The gene wbgl (GenBank accession no. A6M9C2) of the putative α1,2-FucT WbgL of E. coli O126 (UniProtKB/TrEMBL A6M9C2) was synthesized by Geneart® (Regensburg, Germany) including the restriction sites BamHI and XhoI. Ligation into the vector pET22b_his6prop gave the expression vector pET22b_his6propwbgL, which produces His6PropWbgL (513 amino acids) in the cytoplasm of E. coli after induction with IPTG. The gene fkp (UniProtKB/TrEMBL Q58T34) was amplified from genomic DNA of B. fragilis DSM 2151 (DSMZ®, Braunschweig, Germany) using the primers 5′-TTATGATCGTGATACTTGGAATCCCTTATC-3′and 5′-ATGCAAAAACTACTATCTTTACCGTCCAAT-3′. For ligation of the PCR product with the vector pET22b_his6prop, the gene was elongated with BamHI primer 5′-CGCGGATCCGCGATGCAAAAACTACTATCTTTACCG-3′ and XhoI primer 5′-CCGCTCGAGCGGTTATGATCGTGATACTTGG-3′ and finally cloned as described for wbgL.

Cultivation of E. coli JM109(DE3) pET22b_his6propwbgL and E. coli BL21(DE3) pET22b_his6propwbgL
Transformants were grown in 100 mL Erlenmeyer flasks containing 20 mL LB medium with 100 µg/mL ampicillin and incubated overnight at 37°C and 130 rpm. For protein production, cells were grown in 5 L Erlenmeyer flasks with 1000 mL terrific broth medium at 37°C and 80 rpm. The induction of the lacZ promoter was carried out by adding IPTG to a final concentration of 0.1 mM to the cultures (OD600 = 0.6–0.8). Incubation was continued for 20 h at 25°C and the cells were finally harvested by centrifugation.

Enzyme purification
A 40% (w/w) cell suspension of the E. coli cells in 50 mM Tris–HCl buffer pH 7.6 was disrupted by sonication (4 × 15 s). After centrifugation (15,000 rpm, 30 min), the pellets were preserved for the analysis of the production of inclusion bodies by SDS–PAGE. The crude extract (15 mL) was loaded on an IMAC column (1.6 × 20 cm, 1.5 mL/min) using Ni2+–NTA Sepharose (Qiagen®, Hilden, Germany), which was previously equilibrated with 100 mL of 50 mM Tris–HCl pH 7.6 (buffer A). After a washing step with buffer B containing 0.3 M NaCl and 20 mM imidazole proteins were eluted by a concentration of 300 mM imidazole in buffer C (50 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.6, 0.3 M NaCl and 300 mM imidazole). In order to remove imidazole, the IMAC-Pool of the His6PropWbgL diafiltration was performed three times using 50 mL of 50 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.6, in Vivaspin® ultrafiltration unit with a 10 kDa cutoff membrane (Sartorius®, Göttingen, Germany). Protein concentrations of all samples were determined by Bradford assay (Bradford 1976). Fractions were assayed for enzyme activity.

SDS–PAGE and western blot
Expression of His6PropWbgL and His6PropFKP was monitored by SDS–PAGE and western blot. Therefore, SDS–PAGE analysis was performed with 10% acrylamide gels casted according to the gel casting instructions of Invitrogen® (Paisley, UK). Protein samples were loaded onto each slot of the gel. A prestained Protein Ladder PageRuler™ (Fermentas®) was used for the determination of the molecular mass. The protein gels were stained with Coomassie blue.

An immunoblot was performed using a specific anti-His6-antibody in order to detect His6PropWbgL. Therefore, samples of cell debris of E. coli JM109(DE3), crude extract and IMAC fractions of His6PropWbgL were separated on SDS–PAGE gels and transferred onto polyvinylidene fluoride membranes by the NuPAGE® Western transfer protocol (BioRad®, München, Germany). Membranes were blocked with 3% bovine serum albumin in Tris-buffered saline (TBS) buffer (10 mM Tris–HCl, 150 mM NaCl, pH 7.2). A monoclonal anti-His6-antibody conjugated to horse–radish peroxidase (HRP) (Roche Diagnostics®, Mannheim, Germany) was used for specific binding. After a washing step with TBS buffer containing 0.1% Tween-20, the blots were incubated with a 3,3′-Diaminobenzidine substrate (Roche Diagnostics®) and the HRP reaction was stopped by removal of the solution and addition of distilled water.

Activity assays
Enzyme activity of His6PropWbgL in the crude extract and IMAC fractions were determined by a photometric assay (method A) and HPAEC-PAD (method B) for analysis of 2′-fucosyllactose. The photometric assay was performed according to the method described by Barratt using the pyruvate kinase/lactate dehydrogenase system for the detection of released GDP (Barratt et al. 2001). The reaction mixture for the microtiter plate assay contained 2 mM GDP-Fuc, 5 mM lactose, 1 mM phosphoenolpyruvate, 20 mM KCl, 1 mM dithiothreitol (DTT), 0.25 mM reduced nicotineamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH), 2 mM MnCl2, 5 U pyruvate kinase and 5 U lactate dehydrogenase in 50 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.6, in a total volume of 250 µL. The reaction was started by addition of 100 µL enzyme solution and followed at 340 nm at 30°C. Control experiments for the detection of side activities were done without the acceptor substrate lactose. Enzyme activity was also determined by HPAEC-PAD analysis for the detection of 2′-fucosyllactose. The assay solution consisted of 2 mM GDP-Fuc, 5 mM lactose in 50 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.6, containing 2 mM MnCl2, 1 mM DTT and 1 U alkaline phosphatase in a total volume of 175 µL. The reaction solution was incubated at 30°C after the addition of 175 µL crude extract or purified enzyme solution. The reaction was stopped by heating for 5 min at 95°C at different time points where the conversion rate was linear. The centrifuged samples were analyzed by Dionex® HPAEC-PAD (Dionex® Corporation, Sunnyvale, CA) on CarboPac PA1 column using Chromeleon™ 6.40 Software. The elution was carried out with 50 mM NaOH at 30°C (flow rate 1 mL/min, 50 µL injection volume). The concentration of the generated trisaccharide 2′-fucosyllactose was determined by a standard calibration curve with commercial available 2′-fucosyllactose and used for subsequent calculation of enzyme activity. For both HPAEC-PAD and photometric assays, 1 U of His6PropWbgL is the amount of enzyme which produces 1 µmol product (2′-fucosyllactose or GDP) per minute under standard assay conditions.

The activity of the purified fusion protein His6PropFKP was determined using CE-UV for detection of GDP-Fuc (method C): the assay solution of 350 µL contained 8 mM MgCl2, 2 mM GTP, 2 mM ATP, 2 mM l-fucose, 2 U inorganic pyrophosphatase and 100 µL of recombinant His6PropFKP in 50 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.6. Samples at different time points were stopped by heating for 5 min at 95°C and centrifuged for 10 min at 15.000 rpm (Rotina 35R, Hettich, Tuttlingen, Germany). The reaction was monitored for 60 min at 37°C. The formation of GDP-Fuc was monitored by capillary electrophoresis on a P/ACE MDQ apparatus from Beckman Coulter (Krefeld, Germany), equipped with a UV detector. The separation of nucleotide sugars and nucleotides was accomplished in a fused-silica capillary (I.D. 75 mm, 57 cm total capillary length, 50 cm to the detector) with 50 mM Na2B4O7 10H2O buffer, pH 8.9. Conditions for migration and detection were 25 kV (23 mA) at 25°C and UV detection at 254 nm, respectively. Samples were injected by pressure (5.0 s at 0.5 psi in the forward direction). The concentration of the reaction product GDP-Fuc was quantified by a standard calibration curve with commercial available GDP-Fuc. The enzyme activity was determined under linear conversion rate; 1 U of His6PropFKP is the amount of enzyme which produces 1 µmol GDP-Fuc per minute under standard assay conditions.

pH optimum and metal ion dependency
To study the optimal pH value for the activity of recombinant His6PropWbgL, assays were performed at different pH values of a 50 mM Tris–HCl buffer ranging from pH 6.8 to 8.4 at 27°C. Addition of metal ions 2 mM MnCl2, CaCl2, MgSO4 and CoCl2 to standard assays allowed to investigate the metal ion dependency. All samples were analyzed by HPAEC-PAD as described in the section activity assays.

Influence of temperature on enzyme activity and stability
Samples of standard assay reactions were incubated in a range from 25°C to 37°C for 60 min. Enzyme stability of His6PropWgbL was monitored by measuring enzyme activity over a period of 8 days at 27°C in 50 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.6. All samples were applied to HPAEC-PAD analysis.

Kinetic analysis
The kinetic constants for the acceptor substrate lactose and the donor substrate GDP-Fuc were derived from initial rate analysis at a variable substrate concentrations using the photometric assay (Barratt et al. 2001) described before. GDP-Fuc was varied from 0.02 to 4 mM at a constant concentration of 10 mM lactose and lactose was altered from 0.05 to 40 mM at a constant concentration of 2 mM GDP-Fuc. Kinetic constants were determined by non-linear regression analysis according to the Michaelis–Menten equation using the Sigma Plot 10 software (SPSS Science Software GmbH, Erkrath, Germany).

Acceptor substrate spectrum studies
The substrate spectrum of recombinant His6PropWbgL was quantified by a modified assay according to Barratt et al. (2001). Therefore, the concentration of NADH was increased to 2 mM and instead of 5 mM lactose different acceptor substrates were tested to determine the relative activity compared with lactose.

Furthermore, the acceptance of the different substrates were analyzed using HPAEC-PAD, CE-UV or C-HPLC (high-pressure liquid chromatography) analysis in a reaction mixture of 2 mM GDP-Fuc, 5 mM acceptor substrate in 50 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.6, containing 1 U alkaline phosphatase, 2 mM MnCl2, 1 mM DTT and 175 µL purified His6PropWbgL in a total volume of 350 µL. The reaction was stopped by heating for 5 min at 95°C at different time points. Here, the integrity of the results generated with the photometric assay could be confirmed. With decreasing concentration of GDP-Fuc and increasing formation of generated guanosine were monitored with CE-UV method described in the section activity assays (see activity assay method C). The identity of GDP-Fuc and the generated guanosine was confirmed with commercial available substrates. RP-HPLC analysis was carried out on a Dionex LC–System with LiChrospher® 100RP 18–5 µ (CS Chromatographie, Langerwehe, Germany) column. For detection of new compounds, an isocratic method was performed with 15% acetonitrile in water and 0.1% formic acid as a mobile phase at 1.0 mL/min flow rate.

Semi-preparative one-pot synthesis of GDP-Fuc
The synthesis of the nucleotide sugar GDP-Fuc was performed in 50 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.6, containing 8 mM MgCl2, 10 mM GTP, 10 mM ATP, 10 mM l-fucose, 10 U inorganic pyrophosphatase and 2 U His6PropFKP for 4 h at 37°C (10 mL final volume in a 15 mL centrifuge tube). Samples of 80 µL were taken at different time points, enzyme reaction stopped at 95°C for 5 min, centrifuged and analyzed by CE-UV. After complete conversion, the reaction mixture was treated with 10 U alkaline phosphatase for 3 h at 30°C. Enzymes were removed from the reaction mixture by heating for 5 min at 95°C and subsequent centrifugation. Crude reaction products were purified using a Biogel-P2 gel filtration column (1.6 × 90 cm) from BioRad. Milli Q H2O as eluent at a flow rate of 0.1 mL/min. Nucleotide sugar containing fractions (CE-UV) were pooled and concentrated by evaporation. The concentrated product was analyzed by mass spectrometry to confirm the integrity of the synthesized nucleotide sugar. Mass spectrum is depicted in Supplementary Data. The overall yield for the synthesis of GDP-Fuc was 43% (25 mg, 42.5 µmol).

Synthesis of 2′-fucosyllactose in the classical two-step mode
The synthetic reaction of 2′-fucosyllactose was carried out in 50 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.6, containing 8 mM lactose, 1 mM DTT, 4.25 mM GDP-Fuc, 5 U alkaline phosphatase and 2 U His6PropWbgL for 26 h at 27°C (10 mL final volume in a 15 mL centrifuge tube). After complete conversion of GDP-Fuc enzymes were denatured for 5 min at 95°C and removed by centrifugation. Consecutively, reaction products were loaded onto the Biogel-P2 gel filtration column and separated as described in the section for semi-preparative one-pot synthesis of GDP-Fuc. After HPAEC-PAD analysis, fractions containing 2′-fucosyllactose were pooled and concentrated by evaporation for mass spectrometry analysis. The integrity of the compound was verified by ESI-MS as presented in Supplementary Data. The overall yield for the synthesis of 2′-fucosyllactose was 44% (8 mg, 22 µmol).

Synthesis of 2′-fucosyllactose in the sequential reaction mode
In a first step, synthesis of GDP-Fuc was performed as described in the section for semi-preparative one-pot synthesis of GDP-Fuc (700 µL final volume in a 1.5 mL centrifuge tube). During the reaction, samples of 20 µL were taken at different time points, denatured at 95°C for 5 min, centrifuged and analyzed via CE-UV. After complete conversion of l-fucose, the crude reaction products were incubated with 10 U alkaline phosphatase for 3 h at 30°C. After removing of the denatured enzymes, the concentration of GDP-Fuc in the supernatant was quantified by a standard calibration curve as described in the section for semi-preparative one-pot synthesis of GDP-Fuc. In the following step, the crude product solution (step 1), containing 4.3 mM GDP-Fuc, was supplemented with 8 mM lactose, 1 mM DTT, 5 U alkaline phosphatase and 2 U His6PropWbgL and incubated for 22 h at 27°C (700 µL final volume in a 1.5 mL centrifuge tube). At different time points, samples of 70 µL were taken from the reaction vial. The reaction was stopped by heating for 5 min at 95°C and centrifuged before analyzing by CE-UV for detection of residual GDP-Fuc and by HPAEC-PAD for detection of 2′-fucosyllatose.

Mass spectrometry
To confirm the integrity of the compounds, purified products were analyzed by HPLC/ESI mass spectrometry (Thermo Finnigan Surveyor® MSQ™) using the following settings: negative ESI ionization, probe temperature: 400°C; needle voltage: 4.5 kV; cone voltage: 100 V. 10 µL of a 0.1 mM glycan solution were concentrated on a Multospher 120 RP 18 HP-3 μ (60 × 2 mm) and applied at a flow rate of 0.2 mL/min using 50% acetonitrile in water as a mobile phase.

NMR spectroscopy
1H-NMR analysis was carried out in D2O (400 MHz; 30°C) with a Bruker AV 400 Ultra Shield spectrometer. Chemical shifts are given in δ-scale (Trappmann et al.) and coupling constants in Hz. The NMR spectrum and data are depicted in Supplementary Data. They are in accordance with literature data (Urashima et al. 1997).

Contribution of Ser463 residue to the enzymatic and autoprocessing activities of Escherichia coli gamma-glutamyltranspeptidase.

Abstract
A serine residue Ser463, required for proper function of E. coli y-glutamyltranspeptidase (EcGGT) was identified by site-directed mutagenesis on the basis of sequence alignment of human, pig, rat, and three bacterial enzymes. Thr-, Asp-, and Lys-substituted variants were overexpressed in E. coli M15 cells and the recombinant proteins were purified to near homogeneity by nickel-chelate chromatography. With the exception of S463T, the other two variants completely lost GGT activity, implying the importance of this residue in EcGGT. Moreover, substitution of Ser463 with either Lys or Asp impaired the capability of autocatalytic processing of the precursor into alpha- and beta-subunit. Computer modeling showed that the critical bonding distance of Gln390 C-Thr391 OG1 was significantly increased in S463D and S463K, indicating that these distance changes might be responsible for the lack of enzyme maturation. Measurements of intrinsic tryptophan fluorescence revealed alteration of the microenvironment of aromatic amino acid residues in S463D and S463K, while circular dichroism (CD) spectra were nearly identical for wild-type and all mutant enzymes. The temperature-dependent signal in the far-UV region for S463T was consistent with that of wild-type enzyme, but S463D and S463K showed a different sensitivity towards temperature-induced denaturation. These results implied that a significant conformational change occurred as a result of Asp- and Lys-substitution.

γ-Glutamyltranspeptidase (GGT; EC 2.3.2.2) is aheterodimeric enzyme that catalyzes the cleavage ofthe glutamyl linkage of γ-glutamyl compounds andthe transfer of their γ-glutamyl group to other aminoacids and peptides1. The reaction catalyzed by GGT isknown to proceed through a modified ping-pongmechanism2. GGT is found from bacteria to mammalsand is generally considered to be involved in themetabolism of glutathione and in salvaging ofcysteine3-5. In mammals, the enzyme is located on theexterior surface of cells and is composed of amembrane-bound α subunit of 42 kDa, linked non-covalently to a β subunit of 20 kDa6.In E. coli, the α subunit is somewhat smaller(39 kDa) and the entire enzyme is present in the periplasmic space7. Both the α and β subunits of GGTare encoded by a common messenger RNA8-12. Theenzyme is translated as a single chain precursor,which yields subunits post-translationally byautoproteolytic processing13-16. GGT plays a role incellular detoxification through formation ofmercapturic acids and confers resistance againstantitumor drugs17. It is also involved in manyphysiological disorders, such as Parkinson’s disease18,diabetes19 and inhibition of apoptosis20.GGTs belong to the structural superfamily of theN-terminal nucleophilic (Ntn) hydrolases. Membersof this superfamily, despite lacking any discerniblesequence similarity, share the same tertiary fold. Thecore three-dimensional (3D) folding pattern shared byNtn-hydrolases consists of a four-layer αββα-structure with two anti-parallel β-sheets betweenα-helical layers21. Recently, the X-ray structures oftwo bacterial GGTs have contributed greatly to ourunderstanding of the enzyme function. The structureof the acyl-enzyme intermediate of E. coli GGT(EcGGT) confirms the role of Thr391 and the locationof the donor substrate binding site22. Structural evidence has also been provided for the autocatalyticprocessing of EcGGT23, and the recent structure ofHelicobacter pylori GGT has shed still more light onthis mechanism16,24.The availability of both a high resolution crystalstructure22 and a cloned over-expressed gene25 forEcGGT offers the opportunity to investigate the roleof individual amino acids. The recombinant EcGGT istranslated as an inactive 62.4 kDa polypeptideprecursor that undergoes intramolecular autocatalyticcleavage to generate a fully active heterodimercomposed of a 41.2 kDa and a 21.2 kDa subunit25.Recently, we have identified the essential residues forthe enzymatic reaction of EcGGT using site-directedmutagenesis on the conserved Thr407, Asp433 andMet464 residues26. As the replacements Thr407 andAsp433 significantly abolish the enzymatic activity,we presumed both residues to be important for theproper function of EcGGT.Among the serine residues in the β subunit, Ser463of EcGGT is conserved across the GGT family(Fig.1) and has been proposed to be involved in thesubstrate binding22. In the present study, to betterunderstand its role, we used a set of three variants hasbeen constructed by replacing this residue with Thr,Asp or Lys. Mutational analysis has also beenperformed to investigate to show the importance ofSer463 in EcGGT and Lys and Asp replacements onthis position.

Utilisation of 10-formyldihydrofolate as substrate by dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) and 5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR) tranformylase/IMP cyclohydrolase (PurH) in Escherichia coli

ABSTRACT
 
Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) and 5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR) transformylase/IMP cyclohydrolase (PurH) play key roles in maintaining folate pools in cells, and are targets of antimicrobial and anticancer drugs. While the activities of bacterial DHFR and PurH on their classical substrates (DHF and 10-CHO-THF, respectively) are known, their activities and kinetic properties of utilisation of 10-CHO-DHF are unknown. We have determined the kinetic properties (k cat/K m) of conversion of 10-CHO-DHF to 10-CHO-THF by DHFR, and to DHF by PurH. We show that DHFR utilises 10-CHO-DHF about one third as efficiently as it utilises DHF. The 10-CHO-DHF is also utilised (as a formyl group donor) by PurH albeit slightly less efficiently than 10-CHO-THF. The utilisation of 10-CHO-DHF by DHFR is ~50 fold more efficient than its utilisation by PurH. A folate deficient Escherichia coli (∆pabA) grows well when supplemented with adenine, glycine, thymine and methionine, the metabolites that arise from the one-carbon metabolic pathway. Notably, when the ∆pabA strain harboured a folate transporter, it grew in the presence of 10-CHO-DHF alone, suggesting that it (10-CHO-DHF) can enter one-carbon metabolic pathway to provide the required metabolites. Thus, our studies reveal that both DHFR and PurH could utilise 10-CHO-DHF for folate homeostasis in E. coli.

Keywords
folate pathway, one-carbon metabolic pathway, DHF, 10-CHO-DHF, THF, 10-CHO-THF, DHFR, PurH

Introduction
 
The folate pathway is central to the synthesis of purine nucleotides, thymidylate, glycine and methionine (Fig. 1). The enzymes catalysing inter-conversions of the pathway intermediates are highly conserved across the three domains of life [1–7]. Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) catalyses the reduction of 7, 8-dihydrofolate (DHF) to 5, 6, 7, 8-tetrahydrofolate (THF) by utilising NADPH as a cofactor [8–10]. Serine hydroxymethyltransferase (GlyA) catalyses the conversion of serine and THF to glycine and 5, 10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate (5, 10-CH2-THF) [11]. Methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase-cyclohydrolase (FolD), a bifunctional homodimeric protein carries out sequential steps of converting 5, 10-CH2-THF to 5, 10-methenyltetrahydrofolate (5, 10-CH+-THF) followed by the conversion of the later to 10-formyltetrahydrofolate (10-CHO-THF) by its dehydrogenase and cyclohydrolase activities, respectively [12, 13]. Availability of 10-CHO-THF is crucial for glycinamide ribonucleotide transformylase (PurN) and bifunctional enzyme PurH [aminoimidazole carboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR) transformylase and IMP cyclohydrolase] in a de novo pathway of purine nucleotides biosynthesis in bacteria and eukaryotes. Availability of 10-CHO-THF is also vital for formylation of the initiator tRNA (tRNAfMet) in eubacteria and eukaryotic organelles [14–16]. PurH catalyses formylation of AICAR to 5-formyl-AICAR (FAICAR) using 10-CHO-THF as a formyl group donor. FAICAR is then cyclised to form IMP [17].

DHFR plays a central role in the maintenance of cellular pools of folate species which are essential for cellular growth and proliferation. The enzyme is a well known target of methotrexate and trimethoprim (TMP) for inhibiting growth of cancer cells and bacteria. TMP binds to bacterial DHFRs ~105 fold more tightly than to the vertebrate DHFRs. Thus, it is an important antibacterial agent [18]. DHFRs have been extensively studied from many organisms [18] and their kinetic characterisations have also been carried out using DHF, its well known substrate [19–21]. The 10-formyl-dihydrofolate (10-CHO-DHF) is readily utilised in vitro by DHFR of human leukemic cell extract, and is also a bioactive compound [22]. However, the kinetic properties of 10-CHO-DHF utilisation by DHFR, and its bioactivity in bacteria have not been studied.

PurH has been studied extensively as a target of specific inhibitors for the development of anticancer therapeutics [23]. The enzymes reported from human and chicken catalyse both 10-CHO-THF and 10-CHO-DHF [17, 24]. Further, it was hypothesised that 10-CHO-DHF was the in vivo substrate for mammalian PurH [25]. PurH proteins from bacterial and eukaryotic sources reveal several differences when analysed by multiple sequence alignment (Fig. S1, available in the online version of this article) or by comparison of the three dimensional (3D) structure of human PurH (pdb: 1PL0) with the modelled structure of E. coli PurH (EcoPurH) (Fig. S2). However, bacterial PurH proteins have not been studied for their preferences for 10-CHO-DHF and 10-CHO-THF.

In this study, using E. coli as a bacterial model, we carried out in vitro and in vivo studies of E. coli DHFR (EcoDHFR) and EcoPurH to investigate their activities on 10-CHO-DHF. We show that for maintaining folate homeostasis, the folate pathway in E. coli involves recycling of DHF, 10-CHO-DHF and THF.

 
Methods
 
Chemicals, plasmids, DNA oligomers, E. coli strains and their growth
The 7, 8-dihydrofolic acid (DHF), (6S)-5-formyl-5, 6, 7, 8-tetrahydrofolic acid, calcium salt (5-CHO-THF) were from Schircks Laboratories (Jona, Switzerland). Stock solution of 5, 10-CH+-THF was prepared from 5-CHO-THF in acidic solution (0.1 M HCl and 0.1 M β-mercaptoethanol) with minimal light exposure. We prepared 10-CHO-THF from 5, 10-CH+-THF in 50 mM Tris-Cl (pH 7.5), 0.1 M β-mercaptoethanol under N2-sparged conditions on ice. The 10-CHO-DHF was prepared from 10-CHO-THF following air oxidation as reported [26]. The concentrations of DHF, 5, 10-CH+-THF, 10-CHO-DHF, AICAR (Sigma) and NADPH (Sigma) were determined spectrophotometrically using millimolar extinction coefficients (mM−1 cm−1) of 28, 24.9, 34, 12.6, 6.2 at 282, 350, 234, 269 and 340 nm, respectively [26–29].

Cloning and purification of DHFR, PurH, FolD
All plasmid constructs were made using standard genetic engineering techniques. Dihydrofolate reductase (folA) from E. coli was PCR amplified using pBAD-pNTR-FP and pBAD-pNTR-RP primers, digested with SfiI and ligated to pBAD-SfiI (AmpR) at the same sites to generate pBAD-SfiI-folA (p-folA). E. coli folD was cloned in NcoI and BglII sites of pQE60 to generate p-folD (AmpR) [28]. The purH from E. coli was PCR amplified using purH-F and purH-R primers, digested with NdeI and XhoI and ligated to pET28b at the same sites to generate pET28b-purH (p-purH). All constructs were verified by DNA sequencing. For purification of DHFR and PurH, a single colony of Rosetta (DE3) pLysS harbouring either p-folA or p-purH was inoculated into LB medium containing desired antibiotics and grown overnight. Fresh LB (900 ml) was inoculated with 1 % of the overnight culture and grown at 25 °C (37 °C for DHFR purification) until it reached exponential phase. The strain harbouring p-folA and p-purH were induced by arabinose (0.1 %) and isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG, 0.5 mM), respectively and kept for further growth till saturation. The remaining strategy for purification of DHFR and PurH was same as used for purification of EcoFolD [28]. All proteins were purified to near homogeneity (as assessed by SDS-PAGE). The purified DHFR, PurH and FolD proteins were dialysed against 50 mM Tris-Cl (pH 7.6), 10 mM β-mercaptoethanol, 50 % glycerol (v/v) and KCl (50 mM for PurH only) and stored at −20 °C.

Growth curves
E. coli (3–4 biological replicates) were grown in 2 ml LB at 37 °C with or without desired antibiotic(s) as overnight cultures. The cultures were diluted (103) in M9 minimal medium and 200 µl of these diluted cultures were taken into the wells of a honeycomb plate. The plate was placed in automated Bioscreen C growth reader (Oy Growth). The culture growth was measured at OD600 at 1 h intervals. The graphs for growth analysis were prepared using GraphPad Prism in which mean values with standard deviation (SD) were plotted against time.

Enzyme assays and kinetics
His-tagged versions of DHFR, PurH and FolD from E. coli were purified using Ni-NTA columns, and used in the assays. DHFR activity was measured by a spectrophotometric method as done previously [27]. Briefly, DHFR activity was measured by decreases in the absorbance at 340 nm for 30 s in a buffer consisting of 50 mM Tris-Cl (pH 7.5) and 10 mM β-mercaptoethanol at room temperature. The kinetic constants of DHFR for its activity were determined for DHF, 10-CHO-DHF and NADPH. In one set of reactions, concentrations of DHF (1–55 µM) or 10-CHO-DHF (0.2–60 µM) were varied, keeping NADPH (60 µM) and DHFR (67.5 ng) concentrations constant in 500 µl volume. In another set of reactions, the concentrations of NADPH were varied (0.4–150 µM) keeping DHF or 10-CHO-DHF (50 µM) and DHFR (377 ng) concentrations constant in 500 µl volume. The amount of conversion of DHF, 10-CHO-DHF and NADPH to THF, 10-CHO-THF and NADP+, respectively by DHFR was determined at 340 nm using millimolar extinction coefficient of 11.8 mM−1 cm−1 [27]. PurH assay was performed spectrophotometrically in the buffer (50 mM Tris-Cl, pH 7.5, 50 mM KCl, 10 mM β-mercaptoethanol) by measuring the increase in the absorbance at 312 or 298 nm as reported [17, 24, 31] for 30 s at room temperature. The kinetic constants of PurH for 10-CHO-THF/10-CHO-DHF were measured by varying the concentrations from 5 to 300 µM keeping fixed concentration of AICAR (100 µM) and PurH (8 µg). Similarly, the kinetic constants of PurH for AICAR were measured by varying the concentration of AICAR (5 to 100 µM) and keeping the concentration of 10-CHO-THF at 200 µM.

Validation of folate species by HPLC and HPLC-coupled electrochemical detector
Folates were analysed by HPLC-coupled electrochemical detector (HPLC-ECD) as described [32]. We followed a modified protocol for determination of folates by HPLC (Dionex, 3000 ultimate model). In brief, the folates in the reaction mixtures of either DHFR (0.4 µg) or PurH (1.6 µg) assays were acidified with 200 mM HCl and determined by HPLC and HPLC-ECD using 4.6×150 mm C18 column (Dionex). DHF (100 µM), 10-CHO-DHF (100 µM) and 5, 10-CH+-THF (acidified 10-CHO-THF, 150 µM) were determined in HPLC on the basis of their retention times and absorption maxima at 282, 234 and 350 nm, respectively. These folates were also detected using a four-channel detector ECD (CoulArray Model 5600A, ESA) with potentials set at 0, 200, 400, and 600 mV. The mobile phase was 28 mM K2HPO4, pH set to 2.4 with H3PO4 (Buffer A) and 28 mM K2HPO4, 25 % acetonitrile, pH set to 2.4 with H3PO4 (Buffer B). The column was equilibrated with 90 % A and 10 % B buffer. The folates were eluted from the column using first linear gradient of 70 % A: 30 % B for 10 min, second linear gradient of 40 % A: 60 % B for next 40 min, followed by a third linear gradient of 0 % A: 100 % B for the next 10 min at flow rates of 0.5 ml min−1. Detector response was calibrated by using DHF, 10-CHO-DHF and 5, 10-CH+-THF.

 
Results
 
In vivo assessment of DHFR and PurH activities
DHFR is an essential protein in E. coli. However, the folA gene (which encodes DHFR) could be deleted if it was accompanied with an inactivating mutation in thyA [33]. As also noted by the authors [33], in the absence of deficient thyA activity, deficiency of DHFR (folA) will lead to increase in DHF and depletion of 5, 10-CH2-THF, which would adversely affect one-carbon metabolism (Fig. 1). Thus, folA deletion is better tolerated along with an inactivating mutation in thyA. More importantly, to ensure in vivo activity of the plasmid expressed DHFR, we transformed the LH18 strain (NM522 thyA∆folA :: kan) with p-folA plasmid, and checked the growth of the transformants in M9 minimal medium containing thymidine. We noted that LH18 strain harbouring an empty vector (lacking folA) showed only residual growth in M9 medium while the LH18/p-folA strain grew well (Fig. 2a). The ΔpurH strain did not grow in M9 media but it grew when supplemented with adenine (Fig. 2b) or supported with p-purH (Fig. 2c). These observations are consistent with the fact that both folA and purH are essential, and that their growth deficiency phenotypes (in un-supplemented M9 medium) are direct consequences of the gene deletions (and not due to any changes in their genomic loci).

Purification of DHFR, PurH and FolD
E. coli DHFR, PurH and FolD were purified to near homogeneity as single major bands on SDS-PAGE [Fig. S3a (DHFR), S3b (PurH) and S3c (FolD)]. The theoretical molecular weight of His-tagged DHFR is 19.7 kDa. However, the observed molecular weight of DHFR on SDS-PAGE was ~22 kDa.

Kinetic parameters of DHFR and PurH proteins
The kinetic constants of DHFR and PurH activities were determined (Table 2). DHFR utilised both DHF and 10-CHO-DHF as substrates. The turnover number (k cat) of DHFR for DHF (1370±131 min−1) was ~5 fold higher than that for 10-CHO-DHF (275±10 min−1). However, its catalytic efficiency (k cat/K m) for DHF (249±93 min−1 µM−1) was ~2.7 fold better than that for 10-CHO-DHF (92±27 min−1 µM−1). The kinetic constants of PurH for 10-CHO-THF, 10-CHO-DHF and AICAR were also determined. The K m of PurH for 10-CHO-DHF (245±72 µM) is about twice that for 10-CHO-THF (111±27 µM). And, its (PurH) catalytic efficiency (k cat/K m) for 10-CHO-DHF (1.7±1 min−1 µM−1) is ~1.5 times worse than that for 10-CHO-THF (2.6±1.2 min−1 µM−1). The catalytic efficiency (k cat/K m) of DHFR for 10-CHO-DHF (92±27 min−1 µM−1) was ~50 times higher than that of PurH (1.7±1 min−1 µM−1). The Michaelis-Menten graphs for obtaining kinetic constants of DHFR and PurH are shown in Figs S4 and S5, respectively.

Identification of the reaction products of DHFR and PurH by HPLC and HPLC-ECD
DHFR is known to convert DHF to THF [8, 27, 34]. And, PurH is known to convert 10-CHO-THF to THF [35]. However, as shown in Table 2, both DHFR and PurH utilised even 10-CHO-DHF as substrate. To identify the reaction products, we made use of HPLC and HPLC-ECD. Based on the absorbance, retention time and reduction potential, it was observed that DHFR utilised 10-CHO-DHF and formed 10-CHO-THF (detected as 5, 10-CH+-THF in acidic conditions) (compare Fig. 3a vs c and 3b vs d). Similarly, it was observed that PurH utilised 10-CHO-DHF and formed DHF (compare Fig. 4a vs c and 4b vs d). The corresponding HPLC and HPLC-ECD profiles of buffer, standard 5, 10-CH+-THF (Fig. S6), DHF and 10-CHO-DHF (Fig. S7) are shown. Thus, the products (10-CHO-THF and DHF, respectively) formed in the DHFR and PurH assays could be identified as expected. The identity of the products formed in DHFR and PurH assays were further verified by coupled enzyme assays (Fig. S8).

Engineering 10-CHO-DHF uptake complements for folate homeostasis
The in vitro reactions showed that both DHFR and PurH utilised 10-CHO-DHF as substrate to form 10-CHO-THF and DHF, respectively. Thus, to investigate for 10-CHO-DHF utilisation in vivo, we decided to make use of a plasmid borne gene encoding a folate transporter (on p-FBT, TetR) to enable E. coli to obtain folates from the medium [35]. We chose E. coli ∆pabA strain which does not synthesise p-amino benzoic acid (pABA), an essential metabolite for the biosynthesis of folates (Fig. 1). Expectedly, the ∆pabA strain did not grow in M9 media (Fig. 5a). However, it grew when the medium was supplemented with 5-CHO-THF as control (Fig. 5b). The strain showed growth even when the medium was supplemented with 10-CHO-DHF (Fig. 5c). On the other hand, the LH18 strain (∆folA) harbouring p-FBT showed a poor growth in M9 medium. This growth was improved to some extent when supplemented with 5-CHO-THF but not with 10-CHO-DHF (Fig. 5d). Similarly, on the M9 agar medium also, growth enhancement of LH18 was observed when the medium was supplemented with 5-CHO-THF but not when supplemented with 10-CHO-DHF (Fig. S9).

Major physiological importance of folate pathway in ∆pabA strain
The folate pathway is central to the synthesis of purine nucleotides, thymidylate, glycine and methionine. The ∆pabA strain did not grow in M9 minimal media alone or in the medium supplemented with adenine or glycine (Figs 5a and 6a, b). And, while the strain shows a barely detectable growth upon supplementation of the medium with thymine, growth was significant when supplemented with methionine (compare Fig. 6d with 6a, b and c). The ∆pabA strain grew as well as the wild-type strain when supplemented with adenine, glycine, thymine and methionine together (Fig. 6e).

Discussion
 
The folate metabolic pathway has been extensively explored [1–7]. Deletion of either DHFR or PurH from E. coli leads to growth defect in M9 media. The growth of the strains is rescued upon expression of the deleted genes, from a plasmid borne copy. The growth of ΔpurH strain was also rescued upon supplementation of the growth medium with adenine alone (Fig. 2b). As adenine is known to be converted to purine nucleotides via the salvage pathway, the observation suggests a major role of EcoPurH in the biosynthesis of purine nucleotides. DHFR has been well characterised from many organisms using its primary substrate DHF [19–21]. In this study, we investigated for relative utilisation of DHF and 10-CHO-DHF by EcoDHFR. The catalytic efficiency of EcoDHFR (k cat/K m) for DHF (249±93 min−1 µM−1) was only ~2.7 fold higher than that for 10-CHO-DHF (92±27 min−1 µM−1) suggesting even the latter to be a good substrate for EcoDHFR. The catalytic efficiencies of EcoPurH were 2.6±1.2 and 1.7±1 min−1 µM−1 for 10-CHO-THF and 10-CHO-DHF, respectively (Table 2). From in vitro experiments, we observed that DHFR converts 10-CHO-DHF to 10-CHO-THF, and PurH converts 10-CHO-DHF to DHF. These metabolites were identified by HPLC, HPLC coupled ECD and coupled enzymatic assays. From in vivo experiments, we observed that ∆pabA strain grew well in M9 media supplemented with 10-CHO-DHF. This suggests that 10-CHO-DHF is a bioactive metabolite that can enter in one-carbon metabolism and might be converted to other intermediary metabolites for growth. However, as assessed from the longer lag phases, the growth of the wild-type strain was somewhat delayed compared to that of the ∆pabA strain when supplemented with 5-CHO-THF (Fig. 5b) or 10-CHO-DHF (Fig. 5c) suggesting their toxicities to at least some extent, especially when the intermediates of the one-carbon metabolism are not altered (for example, in the wild-type strain). In this context, the GlyA enzyme in the folate pathway is known to be inhibited by 5-CHO-THF [36]. The rescue of growth defect in LH18 upon supplementation with 5-CHO-THF was seen both on the solid and liquid media (Figs 5d and S9). The ∆pabA strain was not observed to grow when the medium was supplemented with adenine alone (Fig. 6a). However, the strain grew when the medium was supplemented with 10-CHO-DHF (Fig. 5c). These observations suggest that 10-CHO-DHF is utilised to not only provide for the purines but also for other essential metabolites of one-carbon metabolism.

Interestingly, the growth of ∆pabA strain (Fig. 6) was rescued better by supplementation of the medium with methionine, a byproduct of one-carbon metabolic pathway (compared to that with glycine or thymine alone). Recently, the critical limitation of methionine and S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) was observed when the folate pathway of Mycobacterium tuberculosis was disrupted. And, the growth of M. tuberculuosis treated with antifolate drug (WR99210) was rescued when the media was supplemented with SAM alone or serine/methionine/glycine together [37]. Thus, it may be that besides the direct need of methionine in protein synthesis, it is crucially needed for the synthesis of SAM used as methyl donor for methylation of various biomolecules that play important physiological roles [38]. The growth of ∆pabA strain, when supplemented with adenine, glycine, thymine along with methionine, was as good as the wild-type strain (Fig. 6e). The observations suggest that in the cell, 10-CHO-DHF is recycled to 10-CHO-THF which in turn generates other folates for the synthesis of purine nucleotides, glycine, thymine and methionine.

Taken together, our study supports a major role of DHFR in the synthesis of THF and 10-CHO-THF, and that of PurH in converting 10-CHO-THF and 10-CHO-DHF to THF and DHF, respectively. Thus, the utilisation of 10-CHO-DHF happens over two steps. Firstly, 10-CHO-DHF is converted to DHF in folate pathway and secondly, to 10-CHO-THF in one-carbon metabolic pathway (Fig. 1). In conclusion, in vivo and in vitro characterisation of EcoDHFR and EcoPurH has allowed for a better understanding of utilisation of 10-CHO-DHF in the synthesis of purine nucleotides, glycine, thymine and methionine.

Hsp31 of Escherichia coli K-12 is glyoxalase III

Summary
Hsp31 encoded by hchA is known as a heat-inducible molecular chaperone. Although structure studies revealed that Hsp31 has a putative catalytic triad consisting of Asp-214, His-186 and Cys-185, its enzymatic function, besides weak amino-peptidase activity, is still unknown. We found that Hsp31 displays glyoxalase activity that catalyses the conversion of methylglyoxal (MG) to d-lactate without an additional cofactor. The glyoxalase activity was completely abolished in the hchA-deficient strain, confirming the relationship between the hchA gene and its enzymatic activity in vivo. Hsp31 exhibits Michaelis–Menten kinetics for substrates MG with Km and kcat of 1.43 ± 0.12 mM and 156.9 ± 5.5 min−1 respectively. The highest glyoxalase activity was found at 35–40°C and pH of 6.0–8.0, and the activity was significantly inhibited by Cu2+, Fe3+ and Zn2+. Mutagenesis studies based on our evaluation of conserved catalytic residues revealed that the Cys-185 and Glu-77 were essential for catalysis, whereas His-186 was less crucial for enzymatic function, although it participates in the catalytic process. The stationary-phase Escherichia coli cells became more susceptible to MG when hchA was deleted, which was complemented by an expression of plasmid-encoded hchA. Furthermore, an accumulation of intracellular MG was observed in hchA-deficient strains.

Introduction
Methylglyoxal (MG) is a highly reactive α-oxoaldehyde and physiological metabolite (Thornalley, 1990). MG is generated by the fragmentation and elimination of phosphate from dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (GA3P) during glucose metabolism (Thornalley, 1996). MG is a toxic electrophile and reacts with cellular macromolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids (Ferguson et al., 1998). Since the high concentrations of MG can cause cell death, detoxification of MG is essential for cell viability and growth. There are several pathways for the cellular degradation of MG. The glyoxalase system, which consists of glyoxalase I and II, catalyses the conversion of MG to d-lactate with S-d-lactoylglutathione as an intermediate (Thornalley, 1990). The glyoxalase I/II system requires a reduced glutathione (GSH), whereas glyoxalase III catalyses the conversion of MG directly to d-lactate without the involvement of GSH (Misra et al., 1995). MG reductase also catalyses the conversion of MG into lactaldehyde, which is sequentially oxidized to l-lactate by aldehyde dehydrogenase (Misra et al., 1996). Furthermore, aldehyde compounds are reduced in cells by aldo-keto reductases, i.e. YafB, YeaE and YghZ proteins, producing acetol from MG (Ko et al., 2005).

A single enzyme, designated glyoxalase III, catalysing the GSH-independent conversion of MG into d-lactate has been reported in Escherichia coli (Misra et al., 1995; MacLean et al., 1998; Okado-Matsumoto and Fridovich, 2000; Benov et al., 2004). This enzyme was inactivated by thiol-blocking reagents and reactivated by thiol-containing agents, indicating the involvement of the thiol group for catalysis (Misra et al., 1995). The importance of thiol group was also supported by its activity reduction in the superoxide dismutase-deficient strain as well as its sensitivity to oxidizing agents, such as superoxide and hydrogen peroxide (Okado-Matsumoto and Fridovich, 2000). Glyoxalase III exhibits lower enzyme activity than the glyoxalase I/II system in vivo, whereas in vitro, the activity of glyoxalase III is higher than that of glyoxalase I/II (MacLean et al., 1998; Okado-Matsumoto and Fridovich, 2000). Interestingly, the activity of glyoxalase III is not elevated in E. coli lacking glyoxalase I (MacLean et al., 1998). The expression of glyoxalase III was dependent on the growth phase, i.e. higher at the stationary phase because of its dependence on rpoS (Benov et al., 2004). Although the glyoxalase III plays a certain role in the degradation of MG, the corresponding gene has not been reported.

As a homodimeric member of the DJ-1/ThiJ/PfpI superfamily, E. coli Hsp31, a hchA gene product, is known as a heat-inducible chaperone with weak aminopeptidase activity (Malki et al., 2005). It is also reported to play a role in the acid resistance of E. coli cells (Mujacic and Baneyx, 2007). The hchA is transcribed from dual promoters recognized by the sigma D and S subunits of RNA polymerase, which is repressed during the exponentially growing cells by H-NS (Yoshida et al., 1993), and the thermal induction of RNA polymerase relies primarily on the relief of the H-NS-mediated silencing of sigma d-dependent transcription (Mujacic and Baneyx, 2006). Additionally, increasing transcript stability was proposed as a mechanism underlying temperature-dependent control of hchA expression (Rasouly et al., 2007).

The crystal structure of Hsp31 indicates a homology with the PfpI family of putative intracellular proteases of archaebacteria and the ThiJ family of eubacteria (Lee et al., 2003). Furthermore, it has an evolutionarily conserved domain with human protein DJ-1, which is associated with early-onset Parkinson's disease (Bonifati et al., 2003). Three classes of Hsp31 orthologues, i.e. Classes I, II and III, have been described based on their sequence similarity (Quigley et al., 2003). The putative catalytic structure, consisting of Asp(Glu)–His–Cys, was found in the single subunit of the Classes I and II, and in the subunit interface of Class III (Quigley et al., 2003). Hsp31 has an alternative catalytic triad (His–Cys–Glu) consisting of His-186, Cys-185 and Glu-77 residues that partially overlap with the previous structure containing Asp-214 instead of Glu-77. (Lee et al., 2003; Quigley et al., 2003). Glu-77 residue, which is strictly conserved among all of the DJ-1/ThiJ/PfpI proteins (Wei et al., 2007), forms a hydrogen bond with Cys-185 (Zhao et al., 2003). Although each Hsp31 monomer was reported to contain a poorly accessible catalytic triad that is responsible for a broad specificity aminopeptidase activity (Malki et al., 2005), its biochemical function and physiological role have remained unknown.

We demonstrate here that E. coli Hsp31 functions as glyoxalase III, catalysing GSH-independent conversion of MG. The nucleophilic cysteine (Cys-185) and adjacent glutamic acid (Glu-77) residues are critical in enzyme catalysis, forming the core of the active site. Our findings provide evidence that there are multiple pathways for removing intracellular oxoaldehydes.

Results
Proteomic characterization of E. coli glyoxalase III
Glyoxalase III was purified from E. coli K-12 strain deficient in the gloA gene through a series of steps as described in Experimental procedures. The procedure involved ammonium sulphate fractionation, heat treatment, gel filtration chromatography, anion exchange chromatography and hydrophobic interaction column chromatography with n-butyl sepharose (Table 1). The protein after final purification had near homogeneous purity (Fig. 1A); thus, the protein was directly used for analysing its biochemical property. Specific activity of purified protein was increased almost 25-fold over the initial crude extract. To identify a gene encoding glyoxalase III, the purified protein was used for peptide mass fingerprint analysis. The possibility of minor contaminants with the same molecular weight was excluded by two-dimensional electrophoresis (2-DE) analyses. The result of the mass analysis for the candidate protein matched with the amino acid sequence of E. coli Hsp31.
